news.title: The logic behind Trump’s ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’ appeal
news.text:
The answer is low-propensity voters. There are a lot of Republican-leaning voters in the 4th District of Iowa who don’t go to the polls for every election, but turned out in 2024 to vote for Donald Trump. They are the kind who probably wouldn’t turn out for a midterm election in 2026 with no Trump on the ballot. The GOP challenge is how to get their votes this time.

“MAGA low-propensity voters are a sizable part of our low-propensity voters,” Jeff Kaufmann, the longtime chairman of the Iowa Republican Party, told me. “There is no way to turn them out without Trump himself. They don’t get out to vote when Trump is not on the ballot.”

Kaufmann asked the president to visit those voters where they live. “I said to the president, there is no mailer, no commercial, that can turn out the MAGA portion of our low-propensity voters,” Kaufmann recalled. Only Trump in person.

Iowa Republicans know this because appealing to low-propensity voters is how they’ve won elections before. “They literally carried our current governor [Republican Kim Reynolds] over the line,” Kaufmann said. “She will tell you that her reelection was because of the 4th District. We don’t win statewide races, not just governor and Senate but attorney general and state auditor, without turnout in the 4th District — especially during a midterm.”

It’s not just in Iowa. On Friday, Trump traveled to Fort Myers, Florida, in a district he won by 31 points. On Saturday, he traveled to Perry, Georgia, in a district he also won by 31 points. And on Sunday, he traveled to Port Huron, Michigan, in a district he won by 32 points.

It’s not that Republicans are in trouble in those places. Far from it. It’s that Trump is aggressively trying to attract the voters who only come out when he is on the ballot — by asking them to vote like he is.

Trump has been widely mocked for asking voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.” The New Yorker said it shows that “only one subject truly animates Donald Trump on the campaign trail, and it is, of course…himself.” The Daily Beast called it a “desperate plea.” And at his rally in Detroit Saturday with former President Barack Obama, Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul el Sayed ridiculed Trump’s visit to Port Huron and sarcastically asked voters, “Please make sure to vote like Donald Trump is on the ballot.”

Despite what he said, it’s probably safe to assume el Sayed does not really want the 9th Congressional District of Michigan, which includes Port Huron, to vote like Trump is on the ballot, since voters there gave the president that 32-point victory in 2024.

There is research showing that a low-propensity voter strategy makes sense in a lot of places. A 2025 report from Pew Research found that nationwide, voters who were eligible to vote in 2020 and 2022 but did not vote, and then did vote in 2024 — those voters leaned strongly toward Trump. He won the 2024-only voters by 55% to Kamala Harris’s 41%. And this was not just a tiny group of people. Pew found that 2024-only voters made up 12% of the entire electorate in the presidential race that year. It made a big difference for Trump.

Now the president is trying to do the same thing in the context of a midterm election. And if Republicans are trying to turn out low-propensity voters, it makes sense to ask them to pretend that Trump is on the ballot. It might not work, or it might not work everywhere. But it is probably the Republican Party’s best shot at the moment. Speaking the day after the Sioux City rally, Jeff Kaufmann said, “I think we accomplished our goal, which was to energize turnout in the 4th District.”

news.title: Democratic Senate Candidate: Trump Did ‘Better Job’ on Border Than Biden
news.text: Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Iowa, said President Donald Trump has done a “better job” on the border than former President Joe Biden, while identifying several areas where he could work with the Republican president if elected next month. “I agree with Trump. He's done a better job on the border than Biden, for sure,” state Representative Turek told ABC News’ Jonathan Karl on This Week when he was asked what he believed the president has done right. "I agree with him that we need to drive private equity out of housing. I would also like to see us drive private equity out of housing, healthcare, and nursing homes. And I agree with him that we should have no tax on tips, overtime, and Social Security." Turek's campaign has also promised cooperation with Trump on immigration. In a campaign advertisement, Turek says: “In the U.S. Senate, I'll work with anyone to fix it, including President Trump, to secure the border, stop the flow of drugs into Iowa.” Turek described himself on Sunday as a “proud moderate” and a “commonsense prairie populist.” He listed his priorities as including a livable wage, affordable housing, healthcare and pharmaceuticals, drinkable water, Iowa’s cancer rate, functioning public schools, infrastructure and addressing corruption. When Karl asked whether he believed the Democratic Party had moved too far to the left, Turek declined to make a broader judgment about the party. “I don't think a lot about the party as a whole,” he said. “I think about myself, and I think about Iowa.” The remarks came as Turek campaigns against Republican Representative Ashley Hinson, who Trump has endorsed, in one of the country's most closely watched midterm races. Trump won Iowa by 13 points in 2024 when he ran against former Vice President Kamala Harris. A Democratic victory in the Hawkeye State could be important to the party’s hopes of winning control of the Senate, with the Associated Press listing the state among Democrats’ best Republican-held pickup opportunities. Turek said on Sunday that he does not “vilify people for voting for Trump,” saying the president had “accurately identified the problem” when he raised concerns about grocery prices, corruption, electricity costs and keeping the country out of “forever wars.” However, he criticized the results under the Trump administration, arguing that there had instead been “more and more consolidation of wealth and power to a handful of individuals.” He has also targeted foreign policy regarding the Iran war and trade tariffs, contending that rising costs have placed a burden on Iowans. Turek also said that he had been independently recognized as one of the Iowa Legislature’s most bipartisan and effective members. He said he had never approached his work through “the guise of tribalism,” instead voting based on his district, his conscience and what he believed was best for Iowa. Newsweek reached out to Turek's campaign by email Sunday for further comment. Hinson's View on the Border and Immigration Hinson said last year during a conference call with reporters that illegal immigration is the top issue she hears about from her constituents. “There are many mechanisms for people to self deport right now," she said, Radio Iowa reported. "The CDP One app, which is allowing for people to maybe have the chance to come back and experience the American dream, I would encourage people to look into what the Department of Homeland Security is offering there. The number one issue I heard about is the border and safety and making sure we’re deporting people who are not here illegally.” Iowa is known for its extensive farms and agricultural production, and when asked if she had concerns over not having enough farm workers if illegal immigrants are deported, the congresswoman said it was important to work toward a solution that provides a legal immigration workforce visa. "This is a workforce visa, not an amnesty issue,” Hinson said. “And we need to make sure we have those legal pathways for people to come here to work in critical industries like agriculture.” Newsweek reached out to Hinson's campaign by email Sunday for further comment. Border Security Becomes Bipartisan Focus Trump has made tougher border enforcement a defining part of his presidency, including continuing his wall along the U.S.-Mexico border that he started in his first term. Turek’s comparison comes after migration at the U.S.-Mexico border surged and peaked during the Biden administration, a development the Associated Press said in a September analysis as a major reason voters returned Trump to the White House. The AP analysis examined federal records containing the self-reported destinations of 4.5 million migrants released into the U.S. after crossing the border, legally or illegally, between October 2018 and July 2025, which fell under Trump's and Biden's administrations. "The number of migrants released in the U.S. after crossing the border from Mexico began climbing during Trump's first term and rose drastically under Biden," the AP wrote in its analysis. "Border crossings fell sharply after Biden introduced severe asylum restrictions in June 2024 and plummeted more after Trump returned to the White House and suspended asylum at the border." James Talarico, a Democrat who is running for a seat in the U.S. Senate in Texas, a border state, has also embraced a tougher border-security message, declaring himself a “border security Democrat” and saying Biden “failed us during his administration by not securing the border." Although Talarico remains sharply opposed to other aspects of Trump's immigration agenda, he has advocated for hiring more Border Patrol agents, expanding surveillance technology and adding immigration judges, and has said he supports physical border barriers in places where they are needed. news.title: Ravi Gupta: Fake Polls Threaten the Midterms—Act Now
news.text:
Political polling has endured a bruising decade, with several major election cycles producing results that missed the mark by substantial margins.

Just before the 2024 presidential election, the respected Des Moines Register poll placed Vice President Kamala Harris ahead of Donald Trump in Iowa, 47 percent to 44 percent. Trump ultimately carried the state by more than 13 percentage points.

More recently, polling in Democratic primary contests in Michigan and Wisconsin also proved dramatically inaccurate, with some surveys missing the final result by double digits.

In Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary, far-left State Representative Francesca Hong was projected to win by roughly 20 points. Instead, she was defeated.

In Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, Abdul El-Sayed was shown with a double-digit advantage. Although he went on to defeat Representative Haley Stevens, his final margin was just one percentage point.

Initially, many assumed the polling failures were made in good faith. The industry has struggled to assemble representative samples as fewer Americans rely on traditional landline telephones.

But recent events suggest the problem may be more troubling than ordinary polling error.

Earlier this week, FiftyPlusOne, a website that analyzes election data, released a detailed investigation into Wedgewood, a relatively new polling company. The report alleged that the firm had fabricated its survey findings.

Wedgewood initially responded with an expletive-laden direct message to FiftyPlusOne co-founder. The firm then issued a statement acknowledging that it had falsified data, arguing that the work was part of “an experimental project” intended to expose weaknesses, limited oversight and the low barrier to entry in today’s polling industry.

That justification was met with widespread skepticism.

If the stated purpose was truly to improve polling standards, critics argued, Wedgewood could have conducted a small number of surveys, revealed the experiment itself and then proposed safeguards against fraudulent polling. There is no indication, however, that the firm intended to disclose its actions voluntarily.

Wedgewood released more than a dozen surveys covering important races. Its numbers were also incorporated into several polling aggregators, including those operated by The New York Times and Nate Silver. These models combine multiple surveys to reduce the effect of individual outliers and produce more dependable estimates.

Both The New York Times and Nate Silver have since removed Wedgewood’s figures from their models. Before that happened, however, the firm’s inclusion gave its polling an appearance of legitimacy.

In June, during a pivotal phase of Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, Wedgewood published a survey portraying El-Sayed as significantly more competitive against Republican Mike Rogers than Democratic rivals Haley Stevens and Mallory McMorrow. The poll also placed El-Sayed ahead in the primary and gave McMorrow just nine percent support.

For me, that particular survey felt especially personal.

I remember being stunned when I saw the results. I supported McMorrow, and several friends who shared that view began arguing that Democrats should consolidate around Stevens, whom many regarded as their second-choice candidate.

On Tuesday, McMorrow issued a lengthy statement arguing that the Wedgewood poll contributed to a drop in donations and triggered a wave of media inquiries asking whether she should abandon the race.

EXPLORE MORE: California Flood Alert Issued as Monster King Tides Sweep In

McMorrow called the episode “a one-two punch” that “killed us.” Her strategist, Lis Smith, wrote that Wedgewood was among the pollsters Abdul El-Sayed cited when responding to criticism that he would be less electable in a general election.

Wedgewood’s true motivations are still unclear, but it should be noted that when their results diverged from the mainstream view, they tended to do so in ways that tilted in a particular ideological direction. Nate Silver also noticed that ‘the most conspicuously out-of-consensus ‘polls’ that Wedgewood did involve strong numbers for progressive candidates.’

These included polls showing far-left Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong leading Republican Tom Tiffany, and another showing Democrat Troy Jackson leading Susan Collins during a critical stretch when Maine Democrats had to decide who would replace Graham Platner on the ballot.

The firm also recently released a poll showing the Democratic Senate nominee in Mississippi as surprisingly competitive. That was followed by a $1.2 million television buy from the Democrats’ Senate Majority PAC.

That pattern demands an investigation into whether Wedgewood’s allegedly fake polling was actually intended to influence the political process.

The firm was founded by a Republican named Jack Sims and a Democrat named Andrew Prater. Sims apparently had credible polling experience, which helped the firm slip past the limited quality-control measures used by aggregation sites.

Could the firm have been ideologically inclined to help far-left progressives? Or was the goal to help Republicans by boosting the least moderate Democrats in their primaries? Were its founders manipulating prediction markets for profit, as some have alleged? Or were they merely mercenaries paid by some outside organization to sway these elections?

These are all questions that I don’t claim to have answers to. But the Federal Election Commission and other relevant regulators should investigate the firm and its founders to determine their true motives.

Former Kamala Harris adviser Mike Nellis called the founders ‘absolute scumbags’ who ‘should be prosecuted to the full extent of the law.’

In the meantime, an electorate already skeptical of the polling industry has been given yet another reason to tune out the surveys. And whether or not these firms were trying to manipulate elections, there’s now a new playbook to use fake polls to try and shape outcomes.

Partisan operatives, foreign adversaries, and prediction market manipulators could follow their example and shape donor, media and voter expectations.

What should we do? The boring technocratic solution is to create better screens for polling aggregators – only accepting surveys from reputable news organizations, higher education institutions and established independent pollsters who disclose their methodologies and verify their sample collection. But as we learned with the 2024 Des Moines Register poll, even veteran pollsters can be wildly off when fraud isn’t involved.

Republican Speaker Mike Johnson has seized on the moment to urge voters to ignore surveys and go vote. It’s in his interest to discount the polls, given how bleak the data has been for the GOP. But I can’t blame anyone for losing trust in an industry that has misled us time and time again.

We used to worry that bad polls could mislead us about who would win. Now we must contend with fake ones that could decide elections.

Ravi Gupta is a former Obama Administration official and host of the Majority 54 and Lost Debate podcasts

news.title: Wikipedia's origin story, warts and all
news.text: By Jennifer Scalia The Last Best Place on the Internet: A Human History of WikipediaBy Richard CookePublished by Norton307 pages $29.99Remember when Wikipedia was seen as a lark, and maybe even a bit of a joke? An online encyclopaedia that could be written and edited by anyone? Wouldn’t it degenerate into a war of all against all, overrun by PR flacks and trolls? Now, 25 years after its founding, Wikipedia is the largest encyclopaedia ever to have existed. The site has more than seven million articles in English and receives an average of 508 million views a day. The old-school utility of its pages makes it look like an earnest rejoinder to today’s poisoned chalices of sleek branding and gaudy AI slop. While social media platforms fuel engagement by egging on users’ baser instincts, Wikipedia still revolves around the quaint pleasures of human curiosity. Instead of enriching a tech billionaire, it is run as a nonprofit. This isn’t to say that it’s been all sunshine and rainbows. As Wikipedia has grown, its rules have proliferated, making it more bureaucratic; it has also become a target in the accelerating culture wars, derided by Elon Musk as “Wokepedia.” But until recently, Wikipedia seemed to occupy the noncombatant’s sweet spot — what the journalist Richard Cooke terms the “no man’s land” between ‘trust the experts’ and ‘do your own research’”. Cooke’s subtitle promises a “human history of Wikipedia”, and though his treatment is conceptually rich — philosophy, literature, and even architecture come into play — his emphasis is on the human, with all the tragedy and comedy that entails.Key to the origin story of Wikipedia was the forebear it replaced: The printed set of hardback encyclopaedia volumes, with their gilt edges and exorbitant prices. Jimmy Wales, Wikipedia’s cofounder, recalls how his family would receive stickers in the mail every year for pasting into their World Book Encyclopaedia — the analog version of an update. Wales grew up to become an options trader and an avid presence in online philosophy discussion groups. He considered himself an Objectivist: Someone who adhered to the philosophy of Ayn Rand. One of the people he encountered was a philosophy lecturer named Larry Sanger, who thought Objectivists were “kind of jerks.” Wales, though, was an exception. He was a good citizen online — “respectful and probing”, in Cooke’s description — and kept thinking about the World Book from his childhood. He hired Sanger to run Nupedia, a free online encyclopedia that launched in March 2000, but its drawn-out editorial process resulted in few articles and hardly any web traffic. Soon, Wales and Sanger started talking about a “wiki” version of Nupedia — the word is Hawaiian for “quick” — and in January 2001 Wikipedia went live. Amid all this congeniality, there was some inevitable unpleasantness. Cooke details the endless debates, both on the site and behind the scenes. Sanger left Wikipedia in 2002. By that point the dot-com crash had taken his salary — Wikipedia was originally supported by a for-profit start-up — but he had continued to volunteer his services as Wikipedia’s “chief instigator”, warning about its “‘anti-elite’ problem” and calling for more aggressive measures to boot out trolls and vandals. Within a couple of years of Sanger’s departure, Wales stopped referring to him as a cofounder, and even edited his own Wikipedia page to remove references to Sanger. Wales later apologised for doing this. As for Wikipedia’s other struggles, they have run the gamut from fraud, hoaxes, good-faith errors, and bad-faith disinformation campaigns to the never-ending tug of war between Deletionists (who want a more curated experience) and Inclusionists (who believe the project should reflect the limitlessness of the internet). There are also, of course, the pedants, who fuss over minute specifics and believe that they are bringing discipline and rigour to the site, while their detractors fault them for exerting disproportionate control through “argument by exhaustion”. This book introduced me to the term “fancruft”, which refers to the tendency of fans to indulge in “mountains of indiscriminate detail” that would be baffling or boring to non-fans. Despite his extensive stores of Wikipedia knowledge, Cooke never succumbs to fancruft in this consistently enjoyable book. Every informational tidbit has been judiciously chosen. Artificial intelligence (AI) has been both a boon and a hazard. Wikipedia has bots that scour for vandalism; it also allows editors to use AI for translations, while banning AI-generated content. Large language models have trained on Wikipedia, taking advantage of its enormous quantities of text, the links it draws among pages and the fact that it exists in multiple languages. Lately, AI summaries have been siphoning off readership, but the threat may be even more profound. Humans, though, continue to be unpredictable counterpoints to the smooth predictability of machines. Toward the end of the book, Cooke calls the divergent paths of Wales and Sanger a “kind of parable”. Wales went one way, endorsing Kamala Harris for president and writing a book about the importance of trust. Sanger went the other, becoming a vaccine sceptic during the pandemic and voting for Donald Trump. That these two wildly different humans could have once shared the same mission is reflected in the last best place on the internet — or what remains of it. As Cooke writes, “Like the United States itself, it was a constitutional experiment in emancipation and trust, incompletely applied.”The reviewer is the nonfiction book critic for The Times ©2026 The New York Times News Service
news.summary: Wikipedia's 25-year journey highlights the enduring value of human knowledge and collaboration amid misinformation, online disputes and the growing influence of artificial intelligence

news.title: MAGA Blogger Nabbed by ICE After Thirsting Over Crackdowns
news.text:
A pro-ICE conservative blogger has been detained by the agency he ardently supports. 

MAGA personality Samuel Sey, who describes himself as a “blogger, a teacher, a pro-life advocate, and a public speaker,” was taken by ICE agents and is currently being held in an Ohio jail. The jail’s website states he was booked on Oct. 21 and is still being held in custody for ICE.

A donation page made on behalf of Sey confirmed he was detained by ICE while traveling. 

“He is a husband, father, school teacher, married to Annie with three beautiful children, and has been living here as a legal resident of the United States from Canada,” the page stated.

The page also stated that his wife is working to get him released on bail “so he can fix any clerical issues that need to be addressed for his legal residence.”

Sey previously announced on social media in 2022 that he had obtained a marriage license to wed his wife, Annie.

The Daily Beast has reached out to DHS for comment. 

Sey, 39, is the author of the blog SlowToWrite. He has been vocal about his support for ICE agents, writing in one social media post, “If you love America, you should support ICE.”

He’s even gone as far as to say that God would actually be against people who protest ICE agents.

“God isn’t just against anti-ICE protestors who persecute Christians while they are worshipping at church. He is also against the idealogy [sic] of anti-ICE protestors,” he wrote in one post. “Christians who condemn the “protestors” but refuse to condemn their ideology should know that.”

In another post, he proclaimed that “ anti-ICE protestors are influenced by Satan.”

After Minnesota mother Renee Good was shot and killed in her car in January, he echoed popular talking points on the right claiming that she was attempting to ram agents with her car, despite video evidence suggesting otherwise. 

“The woman would still be alive if she didn’t try to run the ICE agent over. You can be saddened by her death and admit that it was self-defense,” he wrote.

While he has been largely pro-ICE, Sey is oftentimes critical of President Donald Trump, especially on the president’s ever-changing views on abortion.

One post from 2024 reads: “It’s a sobering sign of God’s judgment on America that although thousands of babies could die because of Trump—he is a significantly better option than Kamala Harris.”

news.title: Brazilians returning to the polls
news.text:
By Alessandra Freitas, CNN

(CNN) — Brazilians are returning to the polls on Sunday to choose between two candidates campaigning on sharply different versions of the country amid growing concerns over crime, corruption, and a broader rightward shift among Latin American voters.

Leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, entered this month’s presidential election as the favorite by nearly every poll, hoping to secure a fourth term and extend a political career that has shaped the country for more than two decades.

He instead has found himself in a runoff with Flávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, whose stronger-than-expected performance in a first round of voting upended predictions and turned one of Latin America’s most prominent left-wing leaders into the election’s underdog.

The octogenarian’s challenge is tosecure another term after a decades-long political career, while Bolsonaro, 45, attempts to keep his first-round momentum and carry itinto a final victory.

The outcome of Sunday’s vote will have repercussions far beyond Brazil. As right-wing governments gain ground across Latin America, the runoff could determine whether the region’s largest country becomes an ally of the Trump administration — if Flavio accomplishes something his father could not in 2022: defeat Lula at the ballot box.

A first-round upset

According to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, Bolsonaro secured 2.2 million votes more than Lula in the first round of voting. Neither candidate reached the majority needed to win outright, forcing both campaigns to compete for a shrinking pool of undecided voters while trying to mobilize their supporters in a country deeply divided over its political future.

The result exposed vulnerabilities in Lula’s reelection bid, from frustration over the cost of living and crime to difficulties mobilizing parts of his traditional base. It also showed that Jair Bolsonaro’s movement remains strong, even as the former president serves a prison sentence for attempting to overturn his 2022 defeat.

Crime, the economy and last-minute shifts

Public safety has emerged as one of the defining issues of the campaign. A September Quaest/Pax survey found that 28% of Brazilians saw violence as the country’s biggest problem, followed by corruption at 22% and the economy at 19%.

“That is ground that strongly favors the Bolsonaros, because they have made a tough approach on crime their flagship issue from the beginning,” said Brian Winter, editor-in-chief of Americas Quarterly and vice president of policy at Americas Society/Council of the Americas.

Flávio has promised to designate major criminal factions as terrorist groups, expand prisons and lower the age of criminal responsibility. “Those who think I’m radical on public security haven’t seen anything yet,” he said October 13, adding that even El Salvador’s infamous hardline approach under President Nayib Bukele was not enough.

Lula has struggled to reconcile his party’s traditional positions with demands for tougher action. A widely circulated clip of him saying last year that drug traffickers were also victims of drug users reinforced what Winter called a “longstanding perception that the Brazilian left is soft on crime.” Lula later acknowledged that he had expressed himself poorly.

In last Sunday’s televised debate, Bolsonaro pressed Lula over temporary prison leave. Lula defended rehabilitation but said serious offenders should not qualify, then questioned whether Bolsonaro would pardon his father. Flávio did not respond directly during the exchange, but he has repeatedly said he wants Jair Bolsonaro to accompany him up the presidential palace ramp at his inauguration.

That exchange followed what is seen as the runoff campaign’s most striking shifts: in an effort to appeal to voters, Lula signaled support for lowering the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16 for certain serious crimes, though he opposed including it in a pending constitutional amendment.

Winter described the shift as “as close to anathema as you can get in his workers’ party,” which has opposed such a change for decades.

“Lula is now yielding in the campaign’s final days because he recognizes that this may be his biggest vulnerability,” he said, adding that the change illustrates how far Lula is willing to move toward more conservative voters despite a history of resistance to such measures.

Lula has faced criticism about the state of the economy and affordability. Duringhis first two terms, a commodities boom helped lift millions of Brazilians out of poverty and into the middle class.

This time, many voters say they feel little progress. Lula can point to low unemployment and easing inflation, but those indicators have not changed perceptions forhouseholds struggling with everyday prices.

Winter compared the dynamic to the 2024 US presidential election, when favorable statistics failed to overcome frustration with prices under President Joe Biden and then-Vice President Kamala Harris.

“The headline numbers for the economy look good,” Winter said. “But everyday people keep saying that they don’t feel like the economy is prospering. They feel like their standard of living has declined.”

Still, many voters remain loyal to Lula because of the social gains made during his first two terms, while fearing that a Bolsonaro presidency could roll back social rights.

Flávio has sought to counter those concerns by distancing himself from some traditionally conservative positions. On October 16, Congress promulgated a constitutional amendment ending Brazil’s traditional six-day workweek, gradually reducing the maximum workweek without cutting pay. After previously opposing the proposal, Bolsonaro reversed course and voted in favor.

“This is another case of the Bolsonaros being ideologically flexible enough to get elected,” Winter said. “Both sides are doing this in the race’s final days. It’s breathtaking.”

But if there’s one key group both candidates need to win over, both experts and campaigns agree: it’s women.

Women and religion: two crucial divides

Women account for nearly 53% of registered voters and have been more resistant to Bolsonaro-aligned candidates than men. An October 15 Datafolha survey put Lula ahead among women by 49% to 40%, while Flávio led among men by 52% to 40%.

“Women are the key demographic,” Winter said.

Malu Gatto, an associate professor of Latin American politics at University College London, said the gender gap widened after Jair Bolsonaro emerged in 2018, as men gravitated toward the right and women became more supportive of the Workers’ Party.

Both campaigns have also addressed violence against women, particularly femicide, after several brutal cases drew national attention. Brazil recorded 1,571 femicides in 2025, the highest number since the crime was defined in law in 2015, according to the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety.

According to Gatto, the right traditionally emphasizes tougher criminal penalties for aggressors, while the left places greater emphasis on protection and support for victims, including shelters and specialized services.

In his first televisedadvertisement, Flávio placed his wife and daughters front and center. “At home, they’re the ones in charge. And that’s a good thing,” he said – a notable choice for a political movement whose support has traditionally been stronger among men.

Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro, elected to the Senate this month, has also become key to recruiting women into the Liberal Party. For that reason, a public feud she had with Flávio was one of the most troubling parts of his campaign; although it was later resolved, it underscored the group’s importance in the election.

“Michelle has her own electoral capital, among women and among evangelicals,” Gatto said. “She has legitimacy with women and evangelicals in a way Flávio doesn’t.”

Evangelicals, a growing demographic in the predominately Catholic country, have turned into an important voting bloc for the right. Datafolha found Bolsonaro leading among evangelicals by 62% to 29%, while Lula led among Catholics by 52% to 42%.

The Southeast, Northeast and turnout

Geography will also matter. Roughly 40% of Brazil’s electorate lives in the Southeast, where Flávio won 51.4% of valid votes in the first round, compared with 39.7% for Lula. The right-wing senator carried all four states in the region, including São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro — the country’s three largest electoral states.

Minas Gerais has backed the eventual winner in every direct presidential election since 1989. “Its mix of industrialized cities and poorer rural communities makes it a microcosm of Brazil’s political divisions,” said Lucas Fernandes, a political analyst at consulting firm BMJ.

Lula narrowly beat Jair Bolsonaro there in 2022. This time, Flávio won with 48.24% of valid votes against Lula’s 43.33% — a difference of nearly 590,000 votes.

In Northeast, Lula’s stronghold, his first-round margin was smaller than in previous elections. His share of valid votes in Maranhão fell by nearly five percentage points — the sharpest decline in the region — underscoring the challenge of mobilizing his traditional base.

But the challenge isn’t just changing voters’ minds — it’s mobilizing those who stayed home in the first round.

One in five eligible Brazilian voters abstained, a potentially consequential group in a race where just 2.2 million votes separated the candidates. And with 94% of voters telling Datafolha they had already made up their minds, getting supporters to the polls could prove just as important as persuading the few who remain undecided.

What went wrong for Lula — and what has changed?

The first-round result raised an uncomfortable question for Lula’s campaign and political analysts alike: How did a president who defeated Jair Bolsonaro end up losing to his son, a candidate initially considered less politically appealing than his father?

“I think the most important takeaway is that today’s Brazil is turning right,” Winter said, adding that voters have become “more conservative over the last 10 to 15 years.”

The shift reflects a broader electoral trend across Latin America, where several presidential elections since April 2025 — in Ecuador, Bolivia, Honduras, Chile, Costa Rica, Colombia and Peru — have resulted in victories for right-wing or center-right candidates.

A July Datafolha survey found 44% of Brazilians leaning right or center-right in their political values, compared with 39% on the left or center-left, reversing the balance measured in 2022.

Fernandes points out the prevalence of tactical voting — when voters abandon their preferred candidate for one with a better chance of winning or defeating a rival — as an explanation for the first-round surprise in early October.

“All the alternative candidates, at least the competitive ones, were on the right,” Fernandes told CNN. “So Flávio was much more likely than Lula to benefit from that shift in tactical voting, because he is ideologically much closer to the other candidates who were in the race.”

Another factor, Fernandes said, is the deep rejection of Lula’s Workers’ Party, which runs strong among Brazilians who don’t identify with the Bolsonaro movement but are determined to stop Lula’s reelection. That sentiment is even stronger now than in 2022, when Lula benefited from widespread opposition to Jair Bolsonaro after a presidency marked by controversy over his government’s handling of the Covid-19 pandemic.

Fernandes also points to Lula’s campaign underestimating the importance of social media, while the right has long made it central to its strategy. “The right understood this and applied it on several fronts, not just to Flávio’s candidacy, while the left failed to make that transition,” Fernandes said.

“The most important venue for Brazilian politics today is WhatsApp,” Winter agreed, describing how family groups and private conversations influenced by memes and short videos can shape decisions in the final days of a campaign.

The difference was reflected in campaign spending. According to financial disclosures filed with Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, paid social media was Flávio’s second-largest campaign expense in the first round, and Lula’s sixth-largest.

Corruption and political fatigue

Part of the shift to the right in Brazil is due to the association of the left with corruption, although scandals have shadowed both campaigns.

During Sunday’s debate, Lula challenged Bolsonaro to open his financial records and pressed him over his ties to Daniel Vorcaro, the former head of the collapsed Banco Master, whose alleged connections to powerful figures have embroiled Brazil’s political and judicial establishment, including the Supreme Court. Flávio, meanwhile, accused Lula of corruption and raised allegations involving the president’s eldest son, known as Lulinha. Lula’s previous corruption convictions were annulled in 2021.

On Monday, Lula said he would submit documents to Brazil’s electoral court authorizing the disclosure of his banking and telephone records, along with those of his five children, and said it would release the data if Flávio Bolsonaro did the same for himself, his family, and his businesses. In response, Flávio said he would accept the challenge if Lula also opened the banking and tax records of his former chief of staff and disclosed first lady Janja da Silva’s expenses along with presidential corporate-card spending.

The corruption allegations are deepening political fatiguein Brazil, say experts.“It reinforces the disgust and apathy that Brazilians feel with their political system as a whole,” Winter told CNN.

Beyond Brazil

US President Donald Trump has praised Flávio Bolsonaro’s electoral performance but stopped short of formally endorsing him, even as his administration’s tariffs on Brazil and pressure over Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution have strained relations with Lula.

The tensions surfaced again during Sunday’s debate. Lula accused the Bolsonaro family of aligning itself with US interests at Brazil’s expense, while Flávio rejected the charge and criticized Lula’s foreign policy.

A Bolsonaro victory could bring Latin America’s largest economy closer to the US, particularly on security and organized crime, and strengthen a wave of conservative governments elected across the region. Lula has instead emphasized multilateralism, ties with the Global South and China — Brazil’s largest export market — and his resistance to Trump’s tariff measures as a defense of national sovereignty.

The next president will face a more conservative Congress. A narrow result could also test the country’s stability after Jair Bolsonaro’s attempts to overturn his 2022 defeat led to theJanuary 8, 2023, attacks on government institutions. Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing.

For Lula, a win would mean another political comeback. For Flávio, it would mark the return of his father’s movement to the presidency despite Jair Bolsonaro’s conviction and imprisonment.

news.title: ‘Time Is Running Out’: Netanyahu Warns Of Nuclear Threat  From Iran Ahead Of Israeli Elections
news.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has shared a warning by author Yuval Bloomberg about Iran’s efforts to acquire nuclear weapons, describing the prospect as an existential threat to Israel. Bloomberg argued that the country faced a “real and concrete” danger and said the situation would change fundamentally if Tehran obtained a nuclear weapon. He urged Israel to prioritise what he called completing the mission in Iran, saying domestic disputes were distracting attention from the country’s most pressing security concern ahead of its elections.
‘Existential Threat’
Netanyahu shared Bloomberg’s comments in a post on X on Sunday. Bloomberg said Israel had two years remaining under US President Donald Trump to complete the task in Iran, adding that the future after Trump’s term was uncertain.

He referred to the possibility of Kamala Harris or other leaders taking office in the United States, describing them as potentially mediocre. Bloomberg said the time left was crucial to safeguarding Israel’s physical survival and that the country’s essential resources should be directed towards the mission.
He also dismissed domestic controversies, mentioning Qatar, Haredim, conscription and alerts, and said such disputes obscured the larger issue of Iran. He asked what those arguments would matter if two nuclear bombs struck the centre of the country.

Call For Leadership
Bloomberg warned that future generations would not forgive Israel if it failed to seize what he called a historic opportunity to address the threat. He argued that the mission could not be completed under a prime minister who, in his view, was constrained by pressure from the Muslim Brotherhood and people promoting terrorism.
He criticised leadership that he said could not maintain close communication with Trump or withstand pressure from television interviews. His comments framed the issue as an urgent national priority.
Bloomberg acknowledged that some Israelis might strongly dislike Netanyahu, but argued that such opposition would not help address Iran’s nuclear threat. He urged voters concerned about their safety and their families to think carefully before supporting a leader he believes would be unable to complete the mission.

news.title: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer says America is ready to elect a woman
news.text: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer pushed back Sunday on comments made by former first lady Michelle Obama last year that U.S. voters aren’t ready to elect a female president. “Listen, I have got a lot of colleagues who I think are probably interested in running for president, and I’ve heard everyone say, ‘You can’t have this person or that person,’” the governor told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.” “I would put my money on any Democratic governor in the country against [Vice President] JD Vance or [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio in 2028,” she added, pointing to two Republicans widely expected to run for president in two years. Asked directly whether a woman could be the best choice to beat a potential GOP presidential nominee in 2028, Whitmer simply said, “I do.” In 2025, Obama said in public remarks: “As we saw in this past election, sadly, we ain’t ready. That’s why I’m like, don’t even look at me about running, because you all are lying. You’re not ready for a woman. You are not.” Several women, including Whitmer and former Vice President Kamala Harris, are widely speculated to be potential candidates in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary. On Sunday, Whitmer did not deny that she’s exploring a potential run for president in 2028, saying that she’ll decide on her next steps after she departs from her post as governor in January. “When I exit office … I’m going to take a little time off and figure out what I want to do next, so I’ve got nothing new to share with you, unfortunately,” Whitmer told “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker. Earlier this year, Whitmer denied that she planned to run for president but quickly walked back the comments. “There will be a robust group of people running for president,” she said at the time, adding, “I will not be one of them in 2028, I can tell you that.” Later the same day, the governor said: “I never thought I would run for governor. So I guess I should know better to never say never.” Several other Democratic governors, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, are also widely regarded as potential 2028 presidential candidates. Each has been crisscrossing the country ahead of the midterms campaigning on behalf of Democratic gubernatorial candidates in competitive races. Whitmer on Sunday highlighted her support for former public health official Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor in Ohio. Earlier this week, Acton’s opponent, GOP businessman Vivek Ramaswamy, released a TV ad featuring Acton’s mother calling her a “liar.” Acton has publicly shared that she’s been estranged from her mother for nearly 50 years and has accused her late stepfather of sexually abusing her. Acton and her brother were removed from her mother’s custody in 1978 after her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested on a child rape charge. Acton’s mother has not responded to requests for comment. “I’m going to stay focused on getting people like Amy Acton over the finish line. What’s happened to her in Ohio is absolutely abhorrent, and any survivor knows there’s always a backlash. But this is what makes it harder for women to seek help after they’ve been sexually assaulted in this country,” Whitmer said on Sunday. “It is unreal what’s going on, and that’s why we’ve got to — we’ve got to win races like this and elect good people who are going to keep the people at the heart of their work, like Dr. Amy Acton.” Ramaswamy’s decision to air the ad has faced widespread bipartisan condemnation, including from Ohio GOP Sen. Jon Husted, who is locked in a tight re-election race.
news.summary: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer pushed back Sunday on comments made by former first lady Michelle Obama last year that U.S. voters aren’t ready to elect a female president.

news.text:
A rush transcript of "This Week with George Stephanopoulos" airing on Sunday, October 25, 2026 on ABC News is below. This copy may not be in its final form, may be updated and may contain minor transcription errors. For previous show transcripts, visit the "This Week" transcript archive.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

JONATHAN KARL, ABC “THIS WEEK” CO-ANCHOR: Americans are already going to the polls in 47 states. We’re on the trail with the very latest. “THIS WEEK” starts right now.

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

KARL: Nine days to go.

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: We still have to get out and vote.

KARL: Can Republicans defend their home turf?

What would you say to Iowans who are unhappy with Trump’s performance as president?

This morning, my exclusive interviews with the candidates in what may be the closest Senate race in the country.

JOSH TUREK, (D) IOWA SENATE NOMINEE & IOWA SENATE REPRESENTATIVE: We’re a commonsense state that’s masqueraded more red than what we actually are.

REP. ASHLEY HINSON, (R) IOWA SENATE NOMINEE: And I’m not afraid to question somebody in power about something that I disagree with.

KARL: Our report from the Hawkeye state.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: You know, the president’s out there saying China’s paying the tariff, whatever country is paying the tariff, and I have to write a check for thousands of dollars.

KARL: And Maryland Governor Wes Moore on what Democrats should do if they win big on November 3rd.

TRUMP: I only wish I could have had an ad like that against somebody.

KARL: As Trump and Vance defend a controversial ad in the Ohio governor’s race, bipartisan outrage.

HINSON: I think it’s absolutely terrible, and I think they should take the ad down.

KARL: Our roundtable on the ripple effects for the midterms, and maybe even the next race for president.

(END VIDEO CLIP)

ANNOUNCER: From ABC News, it’s “THIS WEEK.” Here now, Jonathan Karl.

KARL: Good morning. Welcome to “THIS WEEK.”

Nine days to go and nearly every sign points in the same direction. Poll after poll shows the president’s approval rating at the lowest of his presidency. Four polls just this week show a record low for Trump. And the non-partisan Cook Political Report keeps moving races towards Democrats, even in deep red South Carolina and Mississippi.

But not a single vote has been counted. And we’ve all seen election surprises. We’ve all seen polls that are wildly wrong as we do what we do, reporting on the races, talking to the experts, talking to the candidates, talking to the voters. It’s worth keeping in mind that none of us really knows how this is going to turn out.

What we do know is that interest is enormous. Early voting is underway in 47 states. About 26 million Americans have already cast ballots. In Georgia, more than a million people voted in the first week alone. The first day breaking a midterm record. In Iowa, Texas, Kansas, we’ve seen signs Democratic enthusiasm and voting is up. Those are states with Republican Senate seats that Democrats hope to flip.

And nine days out, the president is already laying the groundwork to challenge the results. On Thursday, the Justice Department sued to block Alaska from certifying its Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses. Asked about that on Friday, the president said, quote, “I’m the one that said do it.” That’s an extraordinary statement for a president to make. news.title: Moore: Key races in South 'in play,' Democrats 'made mistakes' not investing earlier
news.text:
Gov. Wes Moore (D-Md.) said Sunday that he believes several statewide races in the historically red U.S. South are “in play” for Democrats this cycle, adding that the party has “made mistakes in not investing earlier” in the region.

“We've seen some movement, especially in the South -- talk of Florida potentially being in play, Mississippi, South Carolina. Do you think those places are really in play?” asked “This Week” co-anchor Jonathan Karl Sunday, adding, "And if so, did Democrats make a mistake by not investing earlier?”

“They are,” Moore said. “They are in play, and we have made mistakes in not investing earlier. And I don't even think just earlier in this cycle -- I think earlier in this generation.”

Moore said the Democratic Party had largely written off the region, which he said has led to fewer history-making candidates being elected.

“I am the third African American ever elected governor in the history of the United States of America. That's not because I'm the third African American ever qualified. That's because oftentimes there's been chronic underinvestment,” Moore said.

Democrats are increasingly bullish about their midterm prospects. Polls for top-of-the-ticket races in Texas, Iowa, Kansas and Alaska have shown the Democratic candidates tied with, or even leading against, Republican contenders. More recent polling suggests that statewide races in places considered to be even more in the GOP’s grip -- like Florida, South Carolina and Mississippi -- are closer than expected.

Moore noted his campaign “personally invested” in Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa’s campaign.

“The wonderful thing that I feel about Gina or Keisha [Lance Bottoms in Georgia] or, or Jermaine Johnson in South Carolina is that they would be history-making candidates, but making history is not the assignment. The assignment is to win,” Moore said. “The assignment is to do things like making sure that we can provide health care for people. The assignment is to make sure that we can end child poverty. The assignment is to make sure that we can raise wages."

"If you can do that, then I think you have really good candidates who don't have a chance to win, but really good chance, have a chance to make life better for the people in their states,” Moore declared.

Moore predicted that Democrats would have the successful election they’re hoping for.

“I think it's not just that the base is, is energized. I think right now the base is [enlarged], and that is, that is important,” he said. “I’m seeing it all over the state of Maryland, where we’re campaigning for re-election. … But I'm also seeing it when I'm out campaigning for other common-sense leaders around the country.”

“People are excited right now because they're looking for leadership that's not just going to push back against this corruption from [President] Donald Trump, but push forward for a new direction,” he added.

While the 2026 midterm election is now nine days away, jockeying for the 2028 presidential election is already underway. Karl pressed Moore on whether he’d be one of the Democrats expected to make a run for the White House.

“You’ve been pretty clear over the past year that you’re not running for president, but you seem to be a little less clear now,” Karl said. “Have you changed your mind on this?”

“You know, no, because I’m very focused on--,” Moore began.

“You haven’t changed your mind? So you’re committed to fulfilling a full term [as governor]?” Karl interjected.

“Yeah, I wouldn't be running for re-election if I was thinking about anything else, to be clear,” Moore said. “My entire focus right now is on the people of Maryland.”

Karl also asked Moore to share a few words that came to mind about other potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidates.

On Sen. Mark Kelly: “Remarkable veteran.”

On former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg: “Remarkably competent.”

On Gov. Josh Shapiro: “Really solid advocate.”

On former Vice President Kamala Harris: “Really decent person and great vice president.”

On Gov. Gavin Newsom: “Strong leader.”

On Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez: “Passionate advocate.”

news.title: Democrat Scott Colom aims for deep-red Mississippi Senate seat
news.text:
Why are major Democrats and Republicans flocking to Mississippi in recent weeks?

In a climate where polls show President Donald Trump's approval ratings cratering, Democrats are unusually optimistic about Scott Colom's chances of flipping the Senate seat held by incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith -- even in deep-red Mississippi.

"We got to have a senator that looks out for Mississippi, that puts Mississippi farmers first, Mississippi small businesses first, represent our values by not allowing corruption to ruin our country and actually delivers on the commitments to put America first," Colom told ABC News in an interview earlier this week.

The incumbent's campaign dismisses the Democratic push as the last-ditch effort of a campaign that will fall short.

Colom is a district attorney for four counties along the Mississippi-Alabama border and a former nominee to become a U.S. district judge. He would be Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

Democrats have argued that Colom's prominent credentials, as well as voter pushback against Republican incumbents and motivation among Democratic-leaning Black voters, could help boost him. Mississippi's population is around 36% Black, according to U.S. Census data.

Colom faces an uphill battle, as Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1982 and voted for Donald Trump in 2024 by around 20 points. ABC News rates the race solid Republican.

But he has gotten the attention of national Democrats; major party figures such as former former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock have campaigned with him. Former President Barack Obama also recorded an ad for him released earlier this month.

Harris, during a rally with Colom on Thursday, told attendees, "I've been in those rooms where there's no cameras, it's senators talking to each other... When you have a voice like his in that room, just think about the impact that's going to have on the decisions coming out of that room. Think about that. This is no ordinary time, and this is no ordinary man."

Colom also went viral online last week after a social video he posted showed Hyde-Smith, during a local news interview from February, saying "You have so many proteins to choose from" while discussing how to deal with higher prices on meat and other goods. In the interview, Hyde-Smith also spoke about working on regulations that would help energy production, and tax incentives to help development.

But it was the proteins part that Colom's campaign seized on, with a punchy video that featured voters mocking the senator's words, with one saying, "Pick another protein ... I'd rather pick another Senator instead." (The campaign has confirmed to ABC News that the video has been turned into a campaign ad.)

French said Colom is running a "disciplined campaign" with messages resonating with voters.

Colom and Hyde-Smith have some history, as she blocked his nomination for federal judge in 2023. She cited his support for transgender rights and having previously been boosted by a George Soros-linked PAC, according to the Mississippi Free Press.

He insists his bid for Senate is not motivated by a desire to get back at her.

"It has nothing to do with the run for me ... as a Christian, I forgive her. It's about the people in Mississippi," Colom told ABC News.

Hyde-Smith dismissed Colom's chances.

"We are confident that Mississippians will once again send Cindy Hyde-Smith back to the U.S. Senate on November 3rd. This is simply Washington insiders making a last ditch effort to give life to Scott Colom's failing campaign," campaign manager Jake Monssen told ABC News in a statement.

Hyde-Smith's supporters may be more motivated after a boost from President Donald Trump, who's set to hold a rally in Mississippi on Monday as part of a swing of campaign rallies mostly in red states.

The Republican National Committee announced the rally around a week after Colom's social video went viral, although Trump and the group have not indicated why they are doing the rally there and Trump has expressed confidence in Hyde-Smith.

Hyde-Smith will be attending the rally, according to her campaign.
news.summary: In a climate where polls show Trump's approval cratering, Dems are optimistic about Scott Colom's chances of flipping Republican senator's seat in deep-red Mississippi.

news.title: Trump Claims Obama's Michigan Rally Was 'Empty': What The Photos Show
news.text: President Trump told supporters that a rally addressed by former President Barack Obama in Detroit, Michigan, was "empty" during his own rally in Georgia. Obama was in Michigan to support Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who is in a close fight with Republican Mike Rogers, and his party’s gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson. Trump’s comments are the latest in a long line comparing his crowd sizes against those of various rivals, and in particular Obama’s, showing the president’s continued interest in this topic. Though the venue was relatively small, Obama’s rally in Cass Technical High School's gym had a good attendance, according to photographs and video shared on social media. Newsweek contacted Cass Technical High School by email, along with Obama’s office via press inquiry form, for comment outside of regular office hours. The White House press office referred Newsweek back to Trump’s comments when contacted. Trump’s Comments During his own rally in Perry, Georgia, on Saturday Trump said: "You know I saw Barack Hussein Obama was in Michigan and the place was empty. And they were saying ‘oh this is a large crowd coming the people are tricking through’ – they don’t talk about my crowds, they never talk about them." Trump has a long record of including Obama’s middle name when mentioning the former president, in what critics argue is an attempt to make him sound more Islamic. Referring to El-Sayed by his middle name Trump added: "And now he’s making a speech for Mohammed today and a massive crowd, a massive crowd has shown up. Where are they? They never talk about my crowd. You know we talk about crowd size. I remember Bernie Sanders he used to get big crowds. He would get like 900 to 1,000 people. I get 35, 40 thousand. They say ‘Bernie Sanders spoke before massive crowd’ and Donald Trump was in town also by the way. I had 40,000 he’d have like 90." What Photographs and Video Show Video shared on X by Molly Ploofkins, a commentator with 164,000 followers on the platform, appeared to show the gymnasium where Obama delivered his speech was packed, though the venue was smaller than the stadiums where both Trump and Obama have previously held rallies. According to Ploofkins, Obama’s rally had both a large in-person and overflow crowd, and she included a photograph showing what appeared to be a packed auditorium for the latter. Farrukh, a progressive commentator who posts about American and British politics, also posted a video purportedly taken from the stage during Obama’s speech on Saturday which showed a packed venue. According to the Michigan Bridge, a local media outlet, Obama’s rally was attended by "a crowd of more than 4,300 people." At the event Obama described November’s midterm elections as a potential "circuit breaker" and the "last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness" from the second Trump administration. Trump Rally Size Interest In January 2017 Trump said the crowd at his first presidential inauguration in Washington, D.C. looked like "a million-and-a half people" with his then press secretary Sean Spicer claiming it was the largest inauguration audience in American history. However photographs shared on social media appeared to show a larger attendance at Obama’s 2009 inauguration. A study by FactCheck.org, an independent body, said: "Side-by-side photos of the 2017 inauguration crowds and 2009 inauguration crowds on the National Mall show a noticeable difference, with 2009’s crowds filling up more of the space, from the perspective of the Washington Monument looking toward the Capitol." In 2024 Trump said the attendance at his January 6 2021 Stop the Steal rally, which ended in his supporters storming Congress in a failed bid to stop the 2020 election results being certified, had a larger attendance than Martin Luther King’s 1963 March on Washington. The U.S. Census has estimated this event, which included the famed ‘I have a dream’ speech, was attended by around 200,000 people. Trump also accused the Kamala Harris campaign of using AI to make a photograph of her crowd look larger, though an investigation by ABC News looking at the metadata concluded this was false. Michigan Polling A poll of 1,185 likely Michigan voters conducted over October 15 to 18 put El-Sayed ahead of Rogers by two points, with 50 percent of the vote against his Republican rival's 48 percent. Similarly an InsiderAdvantage survey of 1,200 likely voters in the state, over October 9-10, had El-Sayed ahead by 48 percent to 46 percent. On Wednesday a polling model produced by Nate Silver, based on recent polls, gave El-Sayed a three percentage point lead in the Michigan senate battle. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Robinson and Trevor Davies
news.summary: High school gym where former President spoke looks packed, and local Michigan media says at least 4,300 people attended.

news.title: Fake polls pushing far-left Democrats are a threat to our elections. The 'scumbags' behind this must be investigated: RAVI GUPTA
news.text:
It's been a rough decade for the political polling industry. Over the past few election cycles, we've seen some significant whiffs.

Days ahead of the 2024 election, Iowa's well-respected Des Moines Register poll showed Vice President Kamala Harris leading Donald Trump, 47 percent to 44 percent. Trump won by more than 13 points.

More recently, in Michigan and Wisconsin Democratic primary races, some surveys were off by double digits.

Far-left State Representative Francesca Hong was supposed to win Wisconsin's Democratic gubernatorial primary by around 20 percentage points. She lost.

Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed was up by double digits in his primary. He eventually defeated Representative Haley Stevens, but by only by a single percentage point.

At first, it seemed those errors were made in good faith, perhaps the result of an industry struggling to track down a representative sample of respondents when so many no longer use landline telephones.

Now it seems the story is taking a darker turn.

Earlier this week, an election data analysis website, FiftyPlusOne, published an extensive investigation into an upstart polling firm named Wedgewood, alleging that the firm had outright fabricated its data.

Wedgewood responded not with a denial but with a direct message to the co-founder of FiftyPlusOne, writing: 'Our official response to your article: *** you.' That, though, was quickly followed by a Wedgewood statement acknowledging that they had faked their data, claiming it was part of 'an experimental project to demonstrate the vulnerabilities, lack of oversight, and overall low barrier to entry in the modern polling industry.'

The explanation was met with appropriate skepticism.

If Wedgewood's goal was to reform the system, perhaps it would have run a few polls early in the cycle, then exposed itself and offered a series of recommendations to protect against phony polling. Yet there is no evidence the firm ever planned to go public on its own.

Wedgewood published more than a dozen polls across key races and its surveys were included in numerous polling aggregators, including those run by The New York Times and Nate Silver, which compile survey results together in the hopes of smoothing out variations and providing more reliable measurements.

The New York Times and Nate Silver have since removed Wedgewood from their models, but at the time, Wedgewood's inclusion gifted them a veneer of credibility.

In June, during a critical stretch of Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, the firm published a poll showing El-Sayed as far more competitive against Republican Mike Rogers than either of his two Democratic opponents, Haley Stevens and Mallory McMorrow. Wedgewood also showed El-Sayed ahead of his primary rivals, including McMorrow, who registered an anemic nine percent in their survey.

That one was personal for me.

I remember seeing this poll and being shocked. I was a McMorrow supporter, and many of my like-minded friends began talking about the need to close ranks behind Stevens, whom most of us considered our second choice.

McMorrow released a lengthy statement on Tuesday detailing how, she believes, the Wedgewood poll caused donations to her campaign to dry up and led to calls from reporters pestering her over calls for her to drop out of the race.

McMorrow described it as 'a one-two punch' that 'killed us.' McMorrow strategist Lis Smith posted: 'Wedgewood was one of the 'pollsters' that @AbdulElSayed leaned on to push back on criticisms that he was less electable in a general election.'

Wedgewood's true motivations are still unclear, but it should be noted that when their results diverged from the mainstream view, they tended to do so in ways that tilted in a particular ideological direction. Nate Silver also noticed that 'the most conspicuously out-of-consensus 'polls' that Wedgewood did involve strong numbers for progressive candidates.'

These included polls showing far-left Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong leading Republican Tom Tiffany, and another showing Democrat Troy Jackson leading Susan Collins during a critical stretch when Maine Democrats had to decide who would replace Graham Platner on the ballot.

The firm also recently released a poll showing the Democratic Senate nominee in Mississippi as surprisingly competitive. That was followed by a $1.2 million television buy from the Democrats' Senate Majority PAC.

That pattern demands an investigation into whether Wedgewood's allegedly fake polling was actually intended to influence the political process.

The firm was founded by a Republican named Jack Sims and a Democrat named Andrew Prater. Sims apparently had credible polling experience, which helped the firm slip past the limited quality-control measures used by aggregation sites.

Could the firm have been ideologically inclined to help far-left progressives? Or was the goal to help Republicans by boosting the least moderate Democrats in their primaries? Were its founders manipulating prediction markets for profit, as some have alleged? Or were they merely mercenaries paid by some outside organization to sway these elections?

These are all questions that I don't claim to have answers to. But the Federal Election Commission and other relevant regulators should investigate the firm and its founders to determine their true motives.

Former Kamala Harris adviser Mike Nellis called the founders 'absolute scumbags' who 'should be prosecuted to the full extent of the law.'

In the meantime, an electorate already skeptical of the polling industry has been given yet another reason to tune out the surveys. And whether or not these firms were trying to manipulate elections, there's now a new playbook to use fake polls to try and shape outcomes.

Partisan operatives, foreign adversaries, and prediction market manipulators could follow their example and shape donor, media and voter expectations.

What should we do? The boring technocratic solution is to create better screens for polling aggregators – only accepting surveys from reputable news organizations, higher education institutions and established independent pollsters who disclose their methodologies and verify their sample collection. But as we learned with the 2024 Des Moines Register poll, even veteran pollsters can be wildly off when fraud isn't involved.

Republican Speaker Mike Johnson has seized on the moment to urge voters to ignore surveys and go vote. It's in his interest to discount the polls, given how bleak the data has been for the GOP. But I can't blame anyone for losing trust in an industry that has misled us time and time again.

We used to worry that bad polls could mislead us about who would win. Now we must contend with fake ones that could decide elections.

Ravi Gupta is a former Obama Administration official and host of the Majority 54 and Lost Debate podcasts
news.summary: We used to worry that bad polls could mislead us about who would win. Now we must contend with fake ones that could decide elections.

news.title: Vucic's mission: Can Serbia's longtime leader secure new mandate? - analysis
news.text: As Serbs head to the polls on Sunday in one of the most consequential elections in the country's recent history, Aleksandar Vucic is asking voters to place their confidence once again in the political leader who has dominated the Balkan country for more than a decade, overseeing a period of considerable economic development while pursuing a distinctive foreign policy that has allowed Serbia to maintain productive relations with the US, Russia, China, and Israel among them. Vucic, who resigned as president on September 27, is seeking to return to the prime minister's office, having served as prime minister between 2014 and 2017 before winning the presidency.This election provides an opportunity to secure a fresh public mandate following almost two years of political unrest, after student-led demonstrations that began after the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad in November 2024, which killed 16 people and prompted widespread accusations of corruption, negligence, and a failure of public accountability.Vucic is the head of a list called United Serbia, made up predominantly of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), a party he helped found almost two decades ago, and the Serbian Radical Party, PUPS, the Serbian People's Party, the Workers' Party, the People's Peasant Party and the United Peasant Party.Despite the two-year-long demonstrations, Vucic enters Sunday's contest with advantages, particularly among voters who associate his leadership with the modernization of Serbia's infrastructure, alongside improvements in living standards, and the stability of a country whose recent history since the breakup of Yugoslavia has been marked by conflict and economic uncertainty.United Serbia coalition leading student-backed list, survey showsAn Ipsos survey published on Thursday placed his United Serbia coalition at 47.4% against 40% for the student-backed list, suggesting the governing bloc retains a sizable electoral base despite the sustained campaign against it. The survey, conducted among 3,624 respondents, was commissioned by Vucic's coalition, while other opinion polls have suggested a considerably closer race or an opposition lead.The outcome remains uncertain, although the figures do indicate somewhat the continuing appeal of a leader whose critics have repeatedly predicted that his political dominance was approaching its end - a situation one may apply to Israel as the country heads to the polls on Tuesday.From an Israeli perspective, Vucic's continued leadership would preserve an important and valued relationship with a European country that has maintained close diplomatic and defense ties with Israel (especially since October 7), frequently taking positions at odds with those of other European governments.During an exclusive interview with The Jerusalem Post at the Presidential Palace in Belgrade last year, Vucic spoke candidly about Serbia's decision to supply Israel with military equipment almost immediately following the October 7 massacre, despite criticism from European leaders.“I am the only one in Europe today dealing in military ammunition with Israel,” he told this writer at the time. “And it is why I am often criticized by colleagues.”Vucic explained that Serbia had moved quickly to assist Israel in the days following the Hamas attacks, expediting the necessary government approvals to enable the transfer of urgently needed military supplies. The relationship has since deepened, with the two countries expanding cooperation in defense technology and military production, including plans for a joint drone manufacturing facility involving Israel's Elbit Systems.The relationship also goes beyond defense cooperation. Trade and investment have grown considerably in recent years, while the two countries have also deepened their diplomatic engagement, culminating in the establishment of a formal strategic partnership earlier this year, which Foreign Minister Marko Djuric told the Post was an “historic step forward.”Vucic: Serbia-Israel relationship rooted in shared history, security challengesVucic has consistently emphasized that Serbia's relationship with Israel is rooted in a shared history and an understanding of the security challenges facing both countries, sentiments he expressed during the interview in Belgrade.“Our ties with Jews and Israelis – this is something different from a historical perspective up to the present day,” he said. “This isn't policy or current politics, no. This is our politics of all times, and it will always have to remain so.”With regard to the United States, Serbia's affinity with US President Donald Trump since his reelection is seen among its population, with a 2024 Gallup International survey finding that 59% of respondents would have supported him over Kamala Harris, the highest figure recorded in Europe. Earlier this month, Trump praised the Serb-US relationship, telling Newsmax Balkans that the two countries enjoyed "very good relations."Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Djuric also launched a strategic dialogue in July covering economic cooperation, security, and energy infrastructure. For Vucic, closer relations with the US are a major development given the troubled history between the two countries, particularly NATO's bombing of Serbia in 1999, while potentially helping Belgrade diversify its dependence on Russia.Serbia has also developed an increasingly close relationship with the United Arab Emirates, where investment and trade, alongside energy cooperation, have strengthened diplomatic ties between Belgrade and Abu Dhabi.Vucic's friendship with UAE President Sheik Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan has become an important component of that relationship, with the Serbian leader expressing solidarity with the Emirates following the outbreak of the war with Iran in February.One can see through these relationships the diplomatic approach Vucic has pursued throughout his leadership: cultivating close ties with Israel, the US, and Arab partners while maintaining longstanding connections with Russia and China, whose investments in Serbian infrastructure and industry remain important to the country's economic development.Sunday's election will also determine whether Vucic can successfully navigate a considerable personal political transition.Having served as prime minister between 2014 and 2017 before winning the presidency, his resignation last month opened the way for a return to the office through which he first consolidated his leadership of Serbia. His decision does carry some political risk, particularly given the strength of the opposition movement, but it is also a reflection of Vucic's confidence that his electoral appeal remains sufficiently strong to secure another governing mandate.For a country of approximately 6.5 million people, Serbia has established a diplomatic presence considerably greater than its demographic or economic weight might suggest, cultivating relationships with major powers and influential Middle Eastern partners while continuing to pursue its own national interests.
