news.title: Obama Slams Ramaswamy Over ‘Cruel’ Campaign Ad; Rallies Democrats
news.text: Former President Barack Obama on Saturday seized on what he described as cruelty and indecency coming from President Donald Trump and his Republican allies, stepping into one of the nation's ugliest midterm fights as he worked to rally Democratic voters in battleground Ohio.Obama took specific aim at Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an advertising campaign featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr Amy Acton. Trump and Vice President J D Vance have also defended the ad, even as Republican leaders across Ohio, including Governor Mike DeWine, have called for its removal."In recent days, we have seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to," Obama said of Ramaswamy, noting that Acton has "spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she has experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness"."There is a decency we should expect out of our public officials," Obama continued. "And I do not know what has happened where the standards of behaviour are so low that somebody could run an ad like that."Obama, 65, who remains the Democratic Party's best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House, was set to campaign in Michigan later on Saturday night. The midwestern battlegrounds will help determine the balance of power in American politics on November 3, when the final votes are cast in the 2026 midterm elections.Obama shared the stage with Acton and former three-term Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown, who is looking to unseat Republican Senator Jon Husted. Although Ohio has become more reliably Republican, it has been a hotly-contested battleground this year. Trump and Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to drum up support for Husted and Ramaswamy. And the controversy over Ramaswamy's ad has ratcheted up the already high temperature.Ramaswamy has defended his decision to press ahead with the ad as fair game. Appearing before Obama, Acton spoke as if addressing Ramaswamy directly. "My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it is not going to work," she said. "Decency still matters." She added: "Mr Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you will not stoop."After wrapping up in Ohio, Obama was heading to a rally in Detroit for Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official who is working to unite the Democratic base in Michigan after winning a divisive primary by less than a percentage point. El-Sayed is running against former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican.Obama's appearance in the city, which is three-quarters Black, could bolster support for El-Sayed among Black voters. In the primary, his opponent Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about six percentage points. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian vice president, campaigned for El-Sayed in September.El-Sayed criticised Obama after his 2012 reelection for not following through on all of his progressive campaign promises, writing that Obama "was not the right choice -- he just wasn't the wrong one". El-Sayed told reporters earlier this month he appreciated the former president, calling him "foundational" to his ability to run for office, but there were still elements of Obama's presidency he disagreed with.Michigan also has open races for governor, attorney general and secretary of state. Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, is slated to appear along with others down the ballot. Benson is running against Republican Rep. John James.Obama will headline a rally in Georgia next week with Senator Jon Ossoff and candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump is slated to speak in Georgia on Saturday. In Ohio, Obama also called out Trump's inability to lower costs, a key campaign promise, noting that the president has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn."I do not know if you have noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation," he quipped. "He should be on HGTV." He went on: "There is gold everywhere. He is got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."The former Democratic president acknowledged that the nation has Trump for another two years, until his term ends. But voters are not stuck with Trump's allies, he said. "We are not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people," Obama said. "After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence ... you get a chance to say enough is enough."

news.title: Kansas Dem Adam Hamilton’s Megachurch Pushes Gender-Neutral Language for Kids Ministry ‘Inspired’ By LGBTQ+ Activist
news.text:
The Church of the Resurrection, led by Kansas Democrat U.S. Senate nominee Adam Hamilton, encouraged the use of gender-neutral terms instead of references to boys and girls to make children “feel welcome,” according to a message provided to Breitbart News that included an image crediting a transgender-identifying singer and LGBTQ activist as one source of inspiration.

“Hey! In follow up from our conversation on Sunday about our words and working towards being more gender neutral so that all kids feel welcome….here is the promised list of words we can start using instead of boys/girls,” the message reads.

The message, provided to Breitbart News, includes an image titled “Gender-Neutral Terms to Address a Group,” featuring dozens of suggested alternatives to gender-specific greetings, including “peep-a-doodles,” “homo sapiens,” “niblings,” “kiddos,” “kitties,” “comrades,” and “folks.”

At the bottom of the image, an attribution reads, “Inspired by @sara.levine1 @themilajam.”

The latter account belongs to Mila Jam, whose full name is Jahmila Adderley. Wikipedia describes Jam as an American transgender singer, songwriter, dancer, actress, and LGBTQ activist.

Jam celebrated becoming the “1st Black Trans Artist to co-headline BOSTON PRIDE” and promoted identifying as nonbinary, writing, “Happy Non-Binary Awareness Week to all my Enby Fam.”

During the 2024 Democratic National Convention, Jam praised former first lady Michelle Obama, writing, “Nothing like witnessing the Queen of ‘Do Something’ in person.” Ahead of the presidential election, Jam expressed support for former Vice President Kamala Harris, sharing a photograph wearing an early-voting sticker alongside the caption “Ready for Madame President.” Following the election, Jam wrote, “When I grow up I wanna be protected I want my rights I want autonomy,” concluding, “Elect WOMEN, not misogyny.”

Hamilton also supported Harris in the 2024 presidential election, acknowledging that he voted for her and contributing $500 to her campaign on July 23, 2024, two days after former President Joe Biden ended his reelection bid.

The children’s ministry message is the latest development to bring scrutiny to Hamilton’s church as the pastor campaigns to unseat incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R-KS) in November.

Breitbart News previously reported that the Church of the Resurrection, the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, partnered with Kansas City PrideFest to sponsor a “Drag Queen Story Time & Gay Pride Festival.” Images identified the church as a 2025 PrideFest sponsor alongside advertisements for the event’s “Youth & Teen Tents,” which promoted stage performances, free books, story time, arts and crafts projects, and other activities.

Hamilton, who has publicly supported affirming same-sex marriage within the United Methodist Church, legal abortion, and Black Lives Matter, questioned traditional interpretations of scripture during a 2015 pastors’ panel hosted by the LGBTQ-affirming Reformation Project. Describing how congregants who came out to him as gay prompted him to reconsider his understanding of the Bible, Hamilton asked, “How much latitude do we have to push back on it? Where can we say, you know, ‘Here I think Paul’s wrong?’” He later argued in a January 2025 sermon that churches prohibiting women from preaching had misinterpreted Paul’s letters.

Hamilton also questioned whether belief in the Virgin Birth is necessary to follow Jesus Christ during an episode of his Making Sense of Faith podcast, despite personally affirming the teaching. “So I say to people who tell me, ‘I’m not really sure I can believe in the Virgin of birth.’ I’m like, ‘That’s okay. I just want you to follow Jesus,’” he said, arguing that the Apostle Paul would have discussed the Virgin Birth more frequently if it were essential to Christianity. The teaching is included in both the Apostles’ Creed and Nicene Creed.

In a separate 2022 sermon titled “Is the Bible True? Is Jesus the Only Way?” Hamilton argued that adherents of other religions could receive salvation through Jesus Christ without recognizing him during their lifetimes. “And when it comes to other faiths, I believe as a Christian that they are going to — when they get to heaven, they’re going to see Jesus and they’re going to say, ‘Ah, it was you all along that I was searching for,’ but I don’t fear that those folks will spend eternity in Hell,” he said. Hamilton cited C.S. Lewis and John Wesley in discussing his understanding of salvation and has separately said the Bible contains “hundreds” of mistakes or errors.

Hamilton also acknowledged during an October CNN interview that church officials should have immediately contacted police after allegations of sexual abuse involving church camp volunteer Scott Moore, who was accused of molesting teenage boys at retreats in 2005 and 2006. “Absolutely. Like, we should have called the police immediately,” Hamilton said, explaining that immediate reporting was not part of the church’s policy at the time. Marshall has accused Hamilton of allowing Moore to return as a counselor after earlier allegations, when another child was allegedly victimized.

In a 2018 sermon, Hamilton referenced Jesus Christ’s warning that those who harm children would be better off having a millstone tied around their necks and being thrown into the sea, applying the passage to migrant family separations during the Trump administration. “When you see news stories where children are crying and they’re being taken away from their parents, you should look at those stories in the light of what Jesus said about what happens when you harm children,” Hamilton said.

During a January 2020 sermon titled “What Would Jesus Say About Climate Change?” Hamilton discussed how beef consumption and cattle production contribute to greenhouse gas emissions. “Some of the things that we grow, because we like to eat them, like cattle, end up producing more carbon dioxide than other crops that we could grow, other forms of food that we could have,” he said. Kansas is the nation’s third-largest beef-producing state, with approximately 5.8 million cattle and 2.9 million residents. Marshall criticized the remarks, while Hamilton’s campaign countered that the senator had previously discussed reducing methane emissions from cattle.

Breitbart News also reported October 18 that Hamilton’s financial disclosure showed a net worth of up to $20 million, a $394,239 annual salary from the Church of the Resurrection, and $417,372.70 in publishing royalties from United Methodist Publishing House. Hamilton also owns a vacation property in Missouri’s Lake of the Ozarks valued at nearly $1 million and a primary residence in Stilwell, Kansas, reportedly valued at approximately $1.4 million. The disclosures have received attention as Hamilton campaigns against the influence of billionaires and special interests in politics.

news.title: Obama Tells Michigan Voters ‘Change Is in the Air’ While Rallying With El-Sayed in Detroit
news.text:
DETROIT—With early voting starting in the final 10 days before polls close on Nov. 3, former President Barack Obama visited the Motor City to boost progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in his fight to become the state’s next U.S. senator.

Obama took the stage Saturday evening at Cass Technical High School in Detroit, urging voters to mobilize in the final days of the race and framing the current national moment as a chance to restore “kindness and compassion” in American politics.

“Yes, we need to lower costs, and we need to put money in people’s pockets, and we need to end this war and stop corruption in Washington. But we’ve also got to re-find our north star,” Obama told the crowd.

“If we don’t return to some of those old-fashioned virtues of honesty and integrity and kindness and compassion … we will continue to fester in anger and division.”

Recalling his multi-decade tenure in politics, Obama said, “I can tell you when an election comes along that just feels a little bit different.”

“It feels like change is in the air. And Michigan, that’s what I’m feeling right now. That’s what you get a chance to do in 10 days,” Obama said, referencing his famous “Change we can believe in” 2008 campaign slogan.

Obama visited Detroit to boost El-Sayed ahead of his Senate race against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, a Democrat who is running to succeed term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, another Democrat.

The former president made a stop in another critical Rust Belt battleground earlier on Saturday, visiting Ohio for the first time since 2018 to campaign with Democrats Sherrod Brown and Amy Acton, who are running for Senate and governor, respectively.

Michigan and Ohio are critical for Democrats’ efforts to retake the Senate from GOP control this year. The Great Lakes State has one of four seats the party must defend while flipping another four from Republicans to reach a majority.

Brown previously served for nearly 20 years in the U.S. Senate before Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno ousted him in the 2024 election. With Brown back on the ballot, Democrats are hoping to flip the seat vacated by Vice President JD Vance and then filled by former Lt. Gov. Jon Husted.

Brown currently leads Husted by 3.3 percentage points in RealClearPolitics’ polling average.

Among his strong performances throughout the Midwest, Obama won Michigan and Ohio in 2008 and 2012, cementing their status as “Blue Wall” states before both swung to President Donald Trump in 2016. President Joe Biden ultimately won Michigan in 2020, but it swung back to Trump in 2024.

Even though a Republican hasn’t won a U.S. Senate election in Michigan in more than 30 years, this year’s race is tight in the final 10 days before Election Day. El-Sayed sits above Rogers by 1.9 percentage points in RealClearPolitics’ polling average. Recent polls have been close, putting the epidemiologist up by only 1 to 2 points over Rogers.

Detroit, with nearly 1.8 million residents across all of Wayne County, will likely be critical to an El-Sayed win. The metropolitan hub usually swings toward Democrats; Kamala Harris netted 62.49 percent of the vote there in 2024, and Biden won 68.32 percent of the vote in 2020.

But Wayne County was one of several areas that favored El-Sayed’s opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), in the August primary. Stevens carried the county by 5.9 percentage points, and performed even better in neighboring Macomb and Oakland counties.

Saturday was Obama’s first visit to Detroit since he campaigned there for Harris in October 2024. It also marked the first day of early voting across the Great Lakes State.

Obama remains fairly popular among the general public compared to other recent presidents, according to a June CNN/SSRS poll.

Roughly 57 percent of Americans view him favorably, compared to 30 percent who view Biden favorably. The other three recent presidents also scored lower on favorability than Obama: President Donald Trump (34 percent), former President George W. Bush (42 percent), and former President Bill Clinton (38 percent).

Obama is almost universally liked among Democrats as well, with 96 percent in the poll expressing a favorable opinion of him.

Years ago, El-Sayed criticized the Obama administration for what he saw as a failure to live up to progressives’ expectations, particularly on healthcare, but has since attributed those remarks to frustrations when he was young.

“I know that President Obama was handed a really difficult set of circumstances, and he did his best,” El-Sayed told NBC News earlier this month.

During his speech Saturday night, El-Sayed championed Obama for working to pass the Affordable Care Act, praising the legislation for expanding access to healthcare.

“His legacy, it continues to offer a guiding light and fitting lessons for the work that is yet to be done. And that work is not just about getting elected, but using your seat to make a difference in the lives of the people you serve,” El-Sayed said.

Trump is campaigning for Rogers in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday afternoon. Remarks are scheduled to begin at 3 p.m. EDT.
news.summary: ‘I can tell you when an election comes along that just feels a little bit different,’ the former president said.
news.author: Jacob Burg

news.title: Obama Campaigns Alongside El-Sayed, Benson In Fiery Michigan Rally
news.text:
DETROIT, Mich. — In his first day of in-person campaigning this cycle, former President Barack Obama skewered President Donald Trump and his administration while calling voters to arms in the Democrats’ arguably highest profile push to boost their candidates for governor and Senate to victory in Michigan. 

“When you find somebody like Abdul El-Sayed, when you find somebody like Jocelyn Benson, when you find people who genuinely care about people, and who have a strong track record, and are offering real solutions, people who are not in this to enrich themselves but to serve, you’ve got to realize how precious that is and you have to deliver for them. We have got to make sure we elect them,” urged Obama.He continued: “Abdul and Jocelyn understand that this election is not about them – it’s about you. It’s about us.”

Obama took the stage alongside secretary of state Jocelyn Benson, who maintains a slight polling edge in her race for governor against Republican challenger Rep. John James, who has previously ran for Senate. 

“I am tired of politicians like my opponent who just do everything Donald Trump tells them to do. I’m tired of Donald Trump embarrassing us on the global stage with corruption and cruelty and chaos. So, Michigan, tonight I’m asking you to join me in saying enough. Enough. Tonight, I’m asking you to roll up your sleeves and work as hard as you can for the next 10 days,” encouraged Benson.

Obama’s boost can prove mission critical for the Democrats’ Senate candidate progressive firebrand Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in garnering support among Black voters, as some worry about lingering resentment from the Uncommitted Movement turning some voters against former Vice President Kamala Harris in her truncated bid for president in 2024. Harris campaigned alongside El-Sayed in late September. 

El-Sayed, who also took the main stage at the Saturday night event, criticized Obama after his 2012 reelection in a HuffPost op-ed, writing Obama “was not the right choice — he just wasn’t the wrong one.” But on Saturday night, both Obama and El-Sayed acknowledged their difference of belief, stressing their morals and ideals bond, not divide, them.

“Disagreeing on means is different from disagreeing on ends, on our goals,” said Obama. “And Abdul shares my values of wanting everybody to get healthcare. He shares my values that if you work hard every day, you should have a living wage.”

The former president “showed us all what elegance, and grace, and determination look like in a politician and he showed me something in myself that apparently I never forgot,” El-Sayed said earlier.

El-Sayed is looking to best Republican candidate Mike Rogers, former congressman and chair of the House Intelligence Committee, for the state’s seat left open by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters. The pair are effectively deadlocked in several major polls, and prominent election forecasters Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss up. If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim Senator. 

El-Sayed pitched Obama as a split-screen foil with Trump, who has been crisscrossing the country for near-daily rallies as Republicans attempt to aggressively rebuff attrition in their Congressional and gubernatorial ranks, and who will be rallying in Michigan less than 24 hours after Obama’s headlining event. 

“Please make sure to vote like Donald Trump is on the ballot. We don’t need that president to come here and tell us, because y’all, we’ve already got our president, and he’s here tonight to remind us of what exactly is on the ballot” said El-Sayed. 

“Trump got us into a war we’ve got no business fighting. President Obama, he contained the nuclear threat without war. Trump’s tariffs costing auto workers their livelihoods. President Obama, he made sure that they didn’t lose their jobs in the worst financial crisis in a century.”

Obama also took time to sear Trump on the skyrocketing price of gas, housing, and healthcare. He chided the administration’s handling of ongoing, and in his estimation, needless tariff battles with “that historical adversary of ours” Canada, and teased Department of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for his focus on the masculinity and power of the troops.

“How much time do you think this man spends in front of the mirror everyday?” Obama chided about Hegseth. “These are not serious people. And we are paying for the price of their lack of seriousness.”

During a gaggle with reporters after the event, both Benson and El-Sayed felt Obama is an effective closer and seemed grateful for his efforts. And other top Democrats in the state welcomed his eleventh-hour boost.

“When Barack Obama comes to Detroit, Democrats win,” Michigan’s junior senator, Elissa Slotkin, told the crowd Saturday. 

Earlier Saturday, Obama campaigned in Ohio alongside the former senator Sherrod Brown, who is trying for his old job, and gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton. He has plans to rally in Georgia with Sen. Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms. Dozens of other high-profile party surrogates, like former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Senators Cory Booker, Raphael Warnock and Bernie Sanders; Rep. Ro Khanna, to name a few, will crisscross the country to boost candidates, and, likely, road-test potential presidential runs. 

The rally also coincided with the first day of early in-person voting in the state. According to a Michigan Democratic official, 4,350 Michiganders were in attendance, between the main venue and the overflow space of Saturday night’s rally.

news.title: Obama seeks to shore up Abdul El-Sayed with Black voters at Michigan rally
news.text: Former President Barack Obama rallied for Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit on Saturday as the bitterly fought contest could come down to the city’s substantial Black vote. “We’re clear about the choice in this election,” Obama said. “Abdul is fighting for change, real change, change that will bring an end to this war. Change that will get money out of politics and put money in your pocket. Change that will finish the job we started with the Affordable Care Act and guarantee quality, affordable healthcare to every single American.” “You hear people say this is somehow radical,” Obama continued. “What is radical about that?” The former president, who rallied earlier Saturday in Cleveland, was joined by El-Sayed, gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson and downballot Democrats less than two weeks before Election Day. Like his speech earlier in the day, Obama lambasted President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans for “broken promises” made during their 2024 campaigns and criticized Trump’s handling of the Iran War and tariffs, both of which he said have had an outsize effect on Michigan. “Does anybody really think this guy is spending that much time thinking deeply on these issues? I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but he is very focused on home renovation. He should be on HGTV,” Obama said of Trump’s extensive changes to the White House. “You remember — roll back the tape, ‘We’re gonna drain the swamp,’” Obama added. “The only thing they drained is the reflecting pool on the National Mall because some no-bid contract got it all messed up.” The Black vote has become a focus in the race as both El-Sayed and his Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., have sought to improve their standing with the critical electorate. Detroit, a city where 75% of the population is Black, is crucial to statewide victories for Michigan Democrats. In the Democratic primary, El-Sayed underperformed there compared to his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich. Speaking ahead of the former president, El-Sayed excoriated Rogers for appearing this Sunday with Trump while contrasting his presidency with Obama’s. “Trump got us into a war we’ve got no business fighting,” El-Sayed said. “President Obama, he contained the nuclear threat without war. Trump’s tariffs costing autoworkers their livelihoods. President Obama, he made sure that they didn’t lose their jobs in the worst financial crisis in a century.” An epidemiologist, El-Sayed has leaned on his experience as health director in both Detroit and Wayne County while touting support from prominent Black Democrats, including former Vice President Kamala Harris; Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga.; Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass.; and Michigan Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist to help him make his case. “Abdul is as Michigan as it gets,” Obama said. “Abdul was born here. He was raised here. Parents in the auto industry … Captain of his high school football and lacrosse and wrestling teams. I mean, he’s just a jock. You see those big guns. That’s why he wears those T-shirts.” Polls have consistently forecast a tight race between El-Sayed and Rogers, showing El-Sayed with a substantial edge over Rogers with Black voters. But the margin matters. A recent YouGov survey of likely general election voters found El-Sayed winning 84% of the Black vote, with Rogers taking 11% — roughly the same spread that Michigan exit polls showed in 2024, when Harris narrowly lost the state to Trump in the presidential election. A Fox News poll of likely voters in late September measured Rogers’ support among Black voters at 22%. NBC News visited an early voting location in Detroit on Saturday, ahead of Obama’s rally. Voters who spoke with NBC News said they were casting ballots for El-Sayed. “I’ll admit that I’ve skipped it before,” Tony Gooden, a Detroit voter, said in an interview of having not voted in prior midterm elections. Gooden added that he felt it was important to vote this fall because of “the state of the economy, the state of our country.” “I feel like somebody needs to put a rein on what’s going on in Washington,” said Gooden. “So I can either sit back on my couch and complain, or I can get on and do something about it.” Mary Waters, a member of the Detroit City Council who backed Stevens in the Democratic primary, said she is not yet committed to either candidate but expressed warmth toward Rogers. She said that skepticism of El-Sayed may stem less from a personal dislike of him and more from tense relationships between the Arab American and Black communities in Detroit. “I don’t think that President Obama himself even understands the racial divides, the class divides, in the city. He does not live here,” Waters said when asked about the impact Obama’s appearance could have, acknowledging that some of her constituents may be swayed by Obama’s pitch. In a recent interview with The Root, an online publication that covers Black news and culture, El-Sayed acknowledged the tensions Waters highlighted. “Most of that spending was spending intended to break my relationship with the Black community,” El-Sayed said of money spent opposing him during the Democratic primary. “And unfortunately, you know, it was not that hard to break, because for too many Black Detroiters, in particular, their experience with somebody who looks like me is not a good one.” “You go into a gas station, you go to a party store, you’re being talked at from behind bulletproof glass,” he continued. “If you’re a woman, you’re being catcalled. … I’ve always tried to be on the right side of that. But I also understand that, like, if that’s your experience with somebody whose name is like mine, that leaves a terrible taste in your mouth.” Gilchrist, meanwhile, told NBC News he thinks little of Rogers’ attempts to woo Black voters and believes Obama’s rally would help unify the party. “He occupies a singular place in our consciousness as Black Americans, and so his voice matters, and his perspective matters,” Gilchrist said. “I do think that that will be incredibly helpful in terms of letting folks know that this is an opportunity for them to mobilize and to make something happen to have the right senator from Michigan.” El-Sayed, though, has previously expressed criticism of Obama, saying he fell short of delivering change. He has explained his thinking in the run-up to Saturday’s rally. “Do you love your dad? Do you agree with everything your dad has ever done?” El-Sayed said after his Grand Rapids debate with Rogers on Oct. 8. “It’s a normal thing to love somebody, to really appreciate all that they’ve done, and to say, ‘Hey, here’s some things I would have done differently.’ But they still did some important things to create opportunity for you. There is no world in which I get to run for office without somebody like President Obama.” Obama addressed the past criticism on Saturday. “Abdul shares my values of wanting everybody to get healthcare,” he said. “He shares my values that if you work hard every day, you should have a living wage, and you should be able, if you’re a young person starting a family, to be able to buy a house that you can afford, and that you shouldn’t have to pay six bucks every time you fill up the tank of gas to get to work. We share those values of making sure everybody gets a fair shot in this society, and that the system’s not just run for those at the top.” Republicans blasted the rally Saturday, painting El-Sayed as an extremist. “The idea that Barack Obama and Jocelyn Benson would share the stage with” El-Sayed “shows that the Democrat Party is not interested in fixing the issues facing Michigan families, and will always put politics over people,” Republican Governors Association communications director Kollin Crompton said in a statement. Speaking ahead of Obama, Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., sought to explain how the battleground state could potentially send both her, a center-left Democrat, and the progressive El-Sayed to the Senate. “The difference these days under this president is not between progressive versus moderate,” she said. “It is between team fight and team flight.”
news.summary: Former President Barack Obama rallied for Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit on Saturday as the bitterly fought contest could come down to the city’s substantial Black vote.

news.title: Obama, in Midwest, assails 'cruelty' and indecency from Trump and his allies in the midterm campaign
news.text:
AgenciesBarack Obama stepped up campaigning for Democrats in Ohio and Michigan, attacking Donald Trump and Republican allies over campaign tactics and economic concerns ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections.

Detroit: Former President Barack Obama on Saturday seized on what he described as cruelty and indecency coming from President Donald Trump and his Republican allies, stepping into one of the nation's ugliest midterm fights as he worked to rally Democratic voters in two Midwestern battlegrounds.First in Ohio, Obama took aim at Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an advertising campaign featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have also defended the ad, even as Republican leaders across Ohio, including Gov. Mike DeWine, have called for its removal."In recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to," Obama said of Ramaswamy, noting that Acton has "spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she's experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness."Later in Michigan, Obama condemned critics of Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, suggesting that they're using his name or his faith to tear him down."We have seen this movie before. I starred in it," Obama told a packed high school gym in Detroit. "I've got a long-form birth certificate to prove it."Live Events"Abdul is as Michigan as it gets," he added.Obama, 65, remains the Democratic Party's best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House. And he's taking his star power on the road in the final days of the midterm elections, which will help determine the balance of power in American politics on Nov. 3.Trump cast his own ballot on Saturday in Florida, where he defended the Ramaswamy ad, which has emerged as a national flashpoint a little more than a week before Election Day."This is a disgrace," Trump said. "The mother said that Amy Acton is a liar, and she's no good. And you know what? I don't think you can get a better reference on that." He added that if his own mother had said anything bad about him, it would be front and center.The Ramaswamy campaign video features Acton's birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her "a liar" and insinuating she has mental health issues.Acton, Ohio's COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur's husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton.The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive. Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.Appearing before Obama, Acton spoke as if addressing Ramaswamy directly."My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it's not going to work," she said. "Decency still matters." She added: "Mr. Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you won't stoop."Although Ohio has become more reliably Republican, it's been a hotly contested battleground this year. Trump and Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to drum up support for Sen. Jon Husted and Ramaswamy. And the controversy over Ramaswamy's ad has ratcheted up the already high temperature.Michigan, too, is a critical state this midterm season, with high-stakes contests for the Senate and governor.While Obama addressed both races, he offered a passionate defense of El-Sayed, a former public health official running against former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican.The former president pushed back against those who call El-Sayed a radical, declaring that "Abdul shares my values." He also acknowledged that El-Sayed was critical of him after his 2012 reelection for not following through on all of his progressive campaign promises.El-Sayed wrote that Obama "was not the right choice - he just wasn't the wrong one.""Some of these folks say, well, you know, Abdul didn't like some of the things you did as president," Obama said in Detroit, wearing a blue shirt with no tie, his sleeves rolled up. "You know who else doesn't agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama. Michelle Obama, about five times a day."Democrats hoped that Obama's appearance in the city, which is three-quarters Black, could bolster support for El-Sayed among Black voters. In the primary, his opponent Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about 6 percentage points. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian vice president, campaigned for El-Sayed in September.Chunnika Hodges, who lives in Detroit and canvassed for El-Sayed on Saturday, said some Black voters are supporting Rogers because they don't think anything has changed after years of voting for Democrats. Some are also wary of El-Sayed because of his progressive policies, Hodges said."We don't lean to the conservative, but we have seen that within our community," Hodges said. "There are conservative Blacks, conservative Democrats."And while Obama talked up Democratic candidates in Ohio and Michigan, he also spoke at length about Trump.He accused the Republican president and his family of rampant corruption and called out his inability to lower costs, noting that Trump has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn."I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation," Obama quipped. "He should be on HGTV." He went on: "There's gold everywhere. He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."The former Democratic president acknowledged that the nation has Trump for another two years, until his term ends. But voters are not stuck with Trump's allies, he said."We're not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people," Obama said. "After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence ... you get a chance to say enough is enough."Obama will headline a rally in Georgia next week with Sen. Jon Ossoff and candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump is slated to speak in Georgia Saturday.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Obama rallies rapturous Michigan crowd for El-Sayed: ‘He’ll finish the job we started’
news.text:
Barack Obama told a Detroit crowd on Saturday that Abdul El-Sayed was “fighting for change, real change, that will get money out of politics and put money in your pocket”, as he threw his weight behind the Democratic Senate candidate and the rest of the ticket on the first day of early voting in Michigan.

Obama said in front of thousands of onlookers at Cass technical high school in Detroit that El-Sayed would “finish the job we started with the Affordable Care Act and guarantee quality, affordable healthcare to every single American”.

The former president headlined the rally for El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate, and secretary of state Jocelyn Benson, the party’s candidate for governor, at an evening event to “get out the vote”.

He accused Donald Trump of “enriching himself and his family”, and said the administration had set a “culture … at the top” of taking favors. “Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this,” he said.

The rally came on the first day of Michigan’s early voting period, with the general election on 3 November. It was also Obama’s first weekend of in-person campaigning during the midterms, which started in Cleveland, Ohio, earlier in the day to stump for the former Ohio senator Sherrod Brown and Democratic nominee for governor Amy Acton earlier in the weekend. He issued similarly scathing remarks aimed at the White House and the GOP.

The Detroit stop is Obama’s first public show of support for El-Sayed, who emerged from a bitter August primary in which the former president stayed on the sidelines. El-Sayed, a doctor and former Wayne county health official, beat the moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens who was riding on the backing of the Democratic establishment and pro-Israel organizations.

Obama was on the offensive against the administration, mocking the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, as “laser-focused” on the “jawline and testosterone levels of our troops”, asking: “How much time do you think this man spends in front of the mirror every day?”

On tariffs, Obama said Trump was toughest on “that well-known evil empire”, referring to Canada, a few minutes’ drive from Detroit across the bridge. “These are the people who gave us Martin Short and maple syrup,” he said.

He even took a jab at Trump’s attempts to renovate the White House. “He should be on HGTV,” Obama said of the many renovations in Washington, including the White House ballroom and the Rose Garden. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

Questions had hung over whether Obama would back El-Sayed at all. El-Sayed, a champion of Medicare for All, had at one point called the Affordable Care Act, Obama’s signature domestic achievement, an incremental fix. The two men spoke by phone after the primary, and El-Sayed has since called Obama a mentor figure.

El-Sayed has the most ground to make up in Wayne county, where Detroit is the county seat, after Stevens beat him there by about 51% to 45% in the August primaries. Obama last campaigned in Detroit – which is more than three-quarters Black – in October 2024 for Kamala Harris, and Harris herself appeared with El-Sayed in Detroit last month.

Republicans have not held a Michigan Senate seat in 25 years, but the party sees the seat as one of its better pickup chances nationwide. El-Sayed faces Mike Rogers, a former congressman endorsed by Donald Trump who lost a 2024 Senate matchup against Democratic senator Elissa Slotkin by less than half a percentage point. The Cook Political Report rates this race a toss-up.

Slotkin, a featured speaker at the rally, told the crowd that “Michigan believes in electing fighters”. And when it came to any disagreements she may have with El-Sayed, she said: “It’s OK because we agree on so much more.”

“We’re putting a check and balance on Donald Trump in the White House,” she said.

A Marist poll of likely voters statewide conducted in mid-October put El-Sayed at 50% and Rogers at 48%, within the margin of error. RealClearPolitics’s average had El-Sayed ahead by about 2.6 points in a similar timeframe.

Trump has attacked El-Sayed throughout the campaign, calling him a “jihadist”, pointing to his middle name and alleging that he had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, which El-Sayed strongly denies, and has created one of the most viral moments of the year. El-Sayed has also faced a barrage of criticism from the establishment wing of the Democratic party over his appearances with leftwing streamer Hasan Piker.

Trump is due in the state himself on Sunday, when he will hold a rally for Michigan Republicans in Port Huron, on the Canadian border. The city said it will be the first presidential visit to St Clair county.

news.text:
Third-party Wyoming gubernatorial candidate Rebecca Bextel told Tucker Carlson during an interview released Saturday that the Republican Party has “imploded” in the state.

Bextel, a former Republican committeewoman who is running under the Constitution Party to be the next governor of the Equality State, cited the late Charlie Kirk’s June 2020 warning during the interview that the state will become “blue” because Democrats will have infiltrated the Republican Party. She notably accused Republican gubernatorial nominee Eric Barlow of being an example of that. (RELATED: How The Left Is Taking Over America’s Reddest State)

Neither Bextel nor Barlow immediately responded to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s requests for comment.

“And so what happens is the Democrats, they really have no say in Wyoming politics, so they all switch over to the Republican Party. We always have conservatives that split the election for the primary and then we end up with the Democrat candidate,” Bextel said. “And that’s exactly what’s happening right now.”

Barlow beat President Donald Trump’s endorsed candidate, Megan Degenfelder, for the Republican gubernatorial nomination on Aug. 18.

“Our candidate for the Republican Party won’t even sign platform pledge to say that they’ll stick with the party 80% of the time,” Bextel continued. “This guy is so radical. He actually testified in front of Congress one time and said we needed to remove our dependence on fossil fuels in favor of a renewable energy model. So, can you imagine a guy like that being in charge of Wyoming, where our bread and butter is the mineral industry and the energy sector?”

Wyoming is the largest coal-producing state in the nation and also has more oil and natural gas producing leases on federal lands than any other state, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. As such, its four leading sources of revenue in 2026 included $12.4 billion from oil drilling and gas extraction, $4.1 billion from petroleum refining, $3.8 billion from gasoline and petroleum bulk stations, and $3.4 billion from coal mining, according to IBISWorld.

“Well … he’s funded by the Democrats — the dark, George Soros-funded money,” Bextel said when Carlson asked how a candidate like that gets the Republican nomination. “That has trickled its way into Wyoming. We’re a very cheap state to buy politically. So, you know, if you look at someone like Vivek Ramaswamy running a 100-million-dollar governor run, I’ll be lucky if I raise a million bucks. But that’s what I’m taking on.”

“He’s not a Republican,” she also said. “And so, I’m running to basically save us from turning into the state of Colorado. If I lose this election, we will be Colorado in four years.”

Trump won Wyoming 72.3% to 26.1% against former Vice President Kamala Harris during the 2024 presidential election.

“We have tons of people, like in Teton County: a guy will run as a Democrat for county commissioner, lose. news.title: The moment Trump shattered his top successor's dreams right to his face
news.text:
President Donald Trump's presumed 2028 successor remains the same, but he appears unwilling to make their path to the GOP nomination a simple one.

In a new piece for The i Paper, reporter and columnist Sarah Baxter outlined the moment this past week when Trump shattered Vice President JD Vance's 2028 "dreams" directly to his face. Before that, her description began during his interview with journalist Mike Halperin on Air Force Two, where Vance insisted that, "if I run, the President will endorse me,” while stressing that the two have not discussed the matter

"You think? The President wasn’t having any of his cheek," Baxter wrote. "Asked if Vance was right about this at a White House event, Donald Trump shook his head."

“Well, I’ll tell you this,” Trump said. “He’s a very talented person, he’s a very good person, but we’ve, literally, I don’t think we’ve ever talked about it.”

Following that remark, Baxter explained, the camera focused in on Vance, who was "looking embarrassed" by the situation.

"No, sir,” Vance responded. “I said that too."

Trump added: "It’s early, very early right now. We have to get through the midterms, see how it goes." Later, during a midterm rally in Iowa, he once again mused about running for an illegal third term in the White House, instead of relinquishing power to a Republican successor.

"I think the law says that I’m not allowed to run again," Trump said. "I studied that phrase forever. Unfortunately, it’s quite concise. Well, the one thing that’s different, they cheated us on the second one, because we won it three times. So I think I have the right to run again."

"Trump can sound like a broken record about this, but he’s convinced himself he’s owed a third term," Baxter wrote. "If Joe Biden could claim to be running for president right up to the wire in summer 2024, Trump is surely thinking: why can’t I pull off the same trick? If nothing else, toying with the idea of a third term and pursuing every (fruitless) legal avenue to secure it once the midterms are over would help to prevent him from becoming a lame-duck president."

She added: "Whenever Trump is faced with an unpleasant decision or legal problem, he adopts the strategy of 'delay, denigrate, deny.' He could spin the question of a third term well into the last two years of his presidency. But this would leave his Vice President in a tight spot. Evidence is mounting that Vance’s heart is not in becoming the next Kamala Harris."

As much as vice presidents are often treated as the presumed successors to the presidents they serve, Baxter noted that in the last 200 years, only one has actually managed to win the presidency right after their boss: George H.W. Bush, following on from Ronald Reagan. While Reagan was still popular by the end of his second term, Trump is "historically underwater with voters," leaving Vance's prospects in shambles.

"Trump is never going to think anyone, least of all his Vice President, could be a better candidate than himself," Baxter concluded. "You can count on him avoiding endorsing a successor for as long as he can get away with it. By the time he does, Vance may find that, like Harris in 2024, it has come too late."

news.title: Obama, In Ohio, Assails 'Cruelty' And Indecency From Trump And His Allies In The Midterm Campaign
news.text:
Former President Barack Obama on Saturday seized on what he described as cruelty and indecency coming from President Donald Trump and his Republican allies, stepping into one of the nation’s ugliest midterm fights as he worked to rally Democratic voters in battleground Ohio.

Obama took specific aim at Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an advertising campaign featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have also defended the ad, even as Republican leaders across Ohio, including Gov. Mike DeWine, have called for its removal.

“In recent days, we’ve seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to,” Obama said of Ramaswamy, noting that Acton has “spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she’s experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness.”

“There’s a decency we should expect out of our public officials,” Obama continued. “And I don’t know what’s happened where the standards of behavior are so low that somebody could run an ad like that.”

Obama, 65, remains the Democratic Party’s best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House. He was set to campaign in Michigan later Saturday night, lending the Democratic Party his star power in midwestern battlegrounds that will help determine the balance of power in American politics next week.

Obama shared the stage with Acton and former three-term Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is looking to unseat Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

Although Ohio has become more reliably Republican, it’s been a hotly contested battleground this year. Trump and Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to drum up support for Husted and Ramaswamy. And the controversy over Ramaswamy’s ad has ratcheted up the already high temperature.

Ramaswamy has defended his decision to press ahead with the ad as fair game. Trump aggressively defended the ad, which has emerged as a national flashpoint in the midterms’ final days, as he voted in West Palm Beach on Saturday.

“This is a disgrace,” Trump said. “The mother said that Amy Acton is a liar and she’s no good. And you know what? I don’t think you can get a better reference on that.” He added that if his own mother had said anything bad about him, it would be front and center.

The Ramaswamy campaign video features Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her “a liar” and insinuating she has mental health issues.

Acton, Ohio’s COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur’s husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton.

The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive. Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.

Appearing before Obama, Acton spoke as if addressing Ramaswamy directly.

“My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it’s not going to work,” she said. “Decency still matters.” She added: “Mr. Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you won’t stoop.”

After wrapping up in Ohio, Obama was heading to a rally in Detroit for Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official who is working to unite the Democratic base in Michigan after winning a divisive primary by less than a percentage point. El-Sayed is running against former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican.

Obama’s appearance in the city, which is three-quarters Black, could bolster support for El-Sayed among Black voters. In the primary, his opponent Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about 6 percentage points. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian vice president, campaigned for El-Sayed in September.

El-Sayed criticized Obama after his 2012 reelection for not following through on all of his progressive campaign promises, writing that Obama “was not the right choice — he just wasn’t the wrong one.”

El-Sayed told reporters earlier this month he appreciated the former president, calling him “foundational” to his ability to run for office, but there were still elements of Obama’s presidency he disagreed with.

Michigan also has open races for governor, attorney general and secretary of state. Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, is slated to appear along with others down the ballot. Benson is running against Republican Rep. John James.

Obama will headline a rally in Georgia next week with Sen. Jon Ossoff and candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump is slated to speak in Georgia Saturday.

In Ohio, Obama also called out Trump’s inability to lower costs, a key campaign promise, noting that the president has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn.

“I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation,” he quipped. “He should be on HGTV.” He went on: “There’s gold everywhere. He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

The former Democratic president acknowledged that the nation has Trump for another two years, until his term ends. But voters are not stuck with Trump’s allies, he said.

“We’re not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people,” Obama said. “After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence … you get a chance to say enough is enough.”

Peoples reported from New York. AP writer Jill Colvin in New York contributed. Ganun is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. “There’s a decency we should expect out of our public officials,” Obama continued. “And I don’t know what’s happened where the standards of behavior are so low that somebody could run an ad like that.”

Obama, 65, remains the Democratic Party’s best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House. He was set to campaign in Michigan later Saturday night, lending the Democratic Party his star power in midwestern battlegrounds that will help determine the balance of power in American politics next week.

Obama shared the stage with Acton and former three-term Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is looking to unseat Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

Although Ohio has become more reliably Republican, it’s been a hotly contested battleground this year. Trump and Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to drum up support for Husted and Ramaswamy. And the controversy over Ramaswamy’s ad has ratcheted up the already high temperature.

Ramaswamy has defended his decision to press ahead with the ad as fair game. Trump aggressively defended the ad, which has emerged as a national flashpoint in the midterms’ final days, as he voted in West Palm Beach on Saturday.

“This is a disgrace,” Trump said. “The mother said that Amy Acton is a liar and she’s no good. And you know what? I don’t think you can get a better reference on that.” He added that if his own mother had said anything bad about him, it would be front and center.

The Ramaswamy campaign video features Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her “a liar” and insinuating she has mental health issues.

Acton, Ohio’s COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur’s husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton.

The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive. Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.

Appearing before Obama, Acton spoke as if addressing Ramaswamy directly.

“My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it’s not going to work,” she said. “Decency still matters.” She added: “Mr. Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you won’t stoop.”

After wrapping up in Ohio, Obama was heading to a rally in Detroit for Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official who is working to unite the Democratic base in Michigan after winning a divisive primary by less than a percentage point. El-Sayed is running against former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican.

Obama’s appearance in the city, which is three-quarters Black, could bolster support for El-Sayed among Black voters. In the primary, his opponent Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about 6 percentage points. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian vice president, campaigned for El-Sayed in September.

El-Sayed criticized Obama after his 2012 reelection for not following through on all of his progressive campaign promises, writing that Obama “was not the right choice — he just wasn’t the wrong one.”

El-Sayed told reporters earlier this month he appreciated the former president, calling him “foundational” to his ability to run for office, but there were still elements of Obama’s presidency he disagreed with.

Michigan also has open races for governor, attorney general and secretary of state. Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, is slated to appear along with others down the ballot. Benson is running against Republican Rep. John James.

Obama will headline a rally in Georgia next week with Sen. Jon Ossoff and candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump is slated to speak in Georgia Saturday.

In Ohio, Obama also called out Trump’s inability to lower costs, a key campaign promise, noting that the president has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn.

“I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation,” he quipped. “He should be on HGTV.” He went on: “There’s gold everywhere. He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

The former Democratic president acknowledged that the nation has Trump for another two years, until his term ends. But voters are not stuck with Trump’s allies, he said.

“We’re not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people,” Obama said. “After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence … you get a chance to say enough is enough.”

Peoples reported from New York. AP writer Jill Colvin in New York contributed. Ganun is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. news.title: Trump Rejects Disastrous Polls: 'I Don't Believe I Could Be Beaten By Anybody'
news.text:
President Donald Trump once again contested the validity of his disastrous approval ratings during a Friday interview with The Washington Examiner ahead of the upcoming midterms.

He specifically dismissed a new RealClearPolitics poll average during the interview that puts his approval at 38.8%.

“It’s fake,” Trump told the Examiner. “It’s fake.”

The president reportedly based that argument on The New York Times’ earlier inclusion of data from Wedgewood Polls, a company that recently admitted to using fabricated numbers, even though the paper specifically noted it didn’t use Wedgewood in calculating his job approval metrics.

“The job approval, they said it’s 37, 38?” Trump told the Examiner. “I’m not at 38.”

When asked what he believes his job approval rating actually is, Trump again boasted about his popularity and said, “I don’t believe I could be beaten by anybody” — before touting his own number: “I think that if I needed it, which I don’t, I think 60.”

The RealClearPolitics average includes polling data from more than a dozen outlets including Rasmussen Reports, Economist/YouGov, Reuters/Ipsos, ABC/The Washington Post/Ipsos, CNN, CNBC, ABC, The New York Times — and Fox News.

The average shows that the president’s current net disapproval rating sits at 60.4%. He is entering the midterms as one of the least popular presidents in American history.

That didn’t stop him from defending himself even further.

“Show him the 99%. Have you seen it?” Trump asked during the interview. He was referring to a September clip of CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten noting that Trump won 99% “of the MAGA GOP vote” in the 2024 election against then-Democratic nominee Kamala Harris.

While Enten has since regularly highlighted how far the president’s approval has fallen, Trump has frequently touted this CNN segment at his ongoing rallies across the country and said Friday, “They did do some nice polls on me, I must say.”

He continued, “If CNN keeps doing those polls, I’ll like them more and more.”
news.author: Marco Margaritoff

news.title: Obama set to spend Saturday on the Democratic campaign trail ahead of midterms
news.text:
Barack Obama will campaign Saturday alongside Democratic candidates for the U.S. Senate in Ohio and Michigan, two competitive states that will help determine control of the chamber, as the former president steps up his role in the midterm elections.

Obama’s first appearance is in Cleveland with former three-term Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is attempting to unseat Republican Sen. Jon Husted. 

Amy Acton, a Democrat campaigning for governor against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, is also set to join the event.

Although Ohio has shifted more reliably Republican, it has been a fiercely contested battleground this year.

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to rally support for Husted and Ramaswamy.

Obama will then travel to Detroit for a rally with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official working to unify Michigan’s Democratic base after winning a competitive primary by under a percentage point. 

El-Sayed is running against Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers.

Obama’s visit to Detroit, which is three-quarters Black, could help build support for El-Sayed among Black voters. 

During the primary, opponent Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about 6 percentage points. 

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian vice president, campaigned for El-Sayed in September.

El-Sayed offered criticism of Obama after his 2012 reelection over unfulfilled progressive campaign promises, writing that Obama "was not the right choice — he just wasn’t the wrong one."

El-Sayed told reporters earlier this month he valued the former president, calling him "foundational" to his path to run for office, though noting elements of Obama's presidency he differed with.

"It’s a normal thing to love somebody, to really appreciate all that they’ve done, and to say, ‘Hey, here are some things I would have done differently,’" El-Sayed said. "But they still did some important things to create opportunity for you."

El-Sayed spoke with Obama on the phone shortly after winning his primary in August.

Michigan also has open contests for governor, attorney general and secretary of state. Democratic nominee for governor Jocelyn Benson is slated to appear with others down the ballot. Benson faces Republican Rep. John James.

Obama will lead a rally in Georgia next week alongside Sen. Jon Ossoff and candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump is scheduled to speak in Georgia on Saturday.

news.title: There Was Only One Way the Democrats Could Blow the Midterms — and Lord Help ‘Em, They’re Doing It!
news.text:
Forget about packing the Supreme Court, banning ICE, or impeaching the president (again): Should they win congress, the Democrats’ shrewdest move would be moving Election Day to September.

‘Cause if elections were held in September, the Democrats would be undefeated. They’d go from the donkeys to the ’72 Dolphins. The Democrats would run the whole country!

But alas, they always peak too early.

Fun fact: In the last FIVE presidential elections, during the month of September, the Democrats have led the “poll of polls” aggregate every flippin’ time.

It’s become a clear PR pattern: The Democrats build momentum, blitz the media, and peak in popularity before Election Day — and sometimes, they’re so far ahead that the Republicans can’t catch up. Sure, the race tightens down the stretch (uncomfortably so), but the Dems still win.

But an awful lot of the time, the donkeys are gassed. There’s nothing left in the tank. 

So their momentum stalls — and the Republicans soar ahead by the first Tuesday of November. The Dems are all out of ammo, all out of energy, and all out of ideas. Victory slips through their fingers hooves.

And once again, the Republicans control the White House, Senate, and/or the House.

That's psychologically unnerving for the Democrats, because they really, truly believe their own press clippings: Everyone hates Trump. Everyone thinks they ought to be in charge. Everything they see, hear, and read reinforces how wonderful they are.

This election belongs to the Democrats!

Then, when they lose, resentment builds. They blame the voters, blame the consultants, blame the DNC, blame Elon Musk’s space lasers, blame Russia, blame social media — and blame everyone but themselves.

Yet this pattern persists, because the Dems won’t address the root cause. (Which is the best possible news for the GOP.)

Because don’t look now, but the donkeys are doing it again: They’re making the exact same mistake — and this time, it could cost them the 2026 midterms.

Between the historic headwinds, President Donald Trump’s dismal approval rating, and sky-high gas prices, the Democrats should win the midterms by a landslide. Since 1934, the president’s party has lost an average of 27 House seats and 3.4 Senate seats in midterm elections. By each and every current metric and historic benchmark, the Democrats should be dominating. 

So the 2026 midterms ought to be a big, beautiful, Blue Tsunami: They’re the ocean; congress is Atlantis.

That’s the Democrats’ expectation — and the catalyst for their error.

The danger in believing your own press clippings is that it distorts your perspective. You overestimate your own popularity, capabilities, and value, which leads to hubris and overreach.

And you also underestimate your opponent.

In Hollywood, it’s why so many celebs crash and burn. On Wall Street, it’s why so many corporations botch acquisitions, misjudge verticals, and lose money on mergers.

And in politics, it’s why the Democrats can’t resist scaring the [expletive] out of the voters.

Because it’s late October, and the Democrats are struggling yet again. They’re gassed. Even in bright blue states such as Michigan, Minnesota, Maine, and New Hampshire, the Republican Senate candidate is either winning outright or within the margin of error. 

There’s a very real risk the Dems could lose all four elections!

The Democrats had a glide path to victory: Don’t be controversial. Don’t interject divisive issues. No trans or wokeisms. Make the election a litmus test on Donald Trump.

The last one was the motherlode. The Democrats already had all the leftists, party loyalists, DSA acolytes, and Trump-haters in their pocket, but if they could position themselves as a vehicle to “send D.C. a message,” they’d gain all the dissatisfied independents, too.

Including those who disagreed with the Democrats’ policies.

Hey, it’s how MAGA ran the table in 2024: Not everyone who voted for Trump supported his platform, either. Plenty voted Republican because Joe Biden’s senility, DNC corruption, and Kamala Harris’ weirdness repulsed them.

The voters wanted a change; Trump was it. He was the “send D.C. a message” candidate. 

The Democrats keep fading down the stretch because they really, truly believe their own press clippings. After all, their friends in the media keep telling them the same thing: Trump is awful, everyone hates him, the future belongs to the donkeys.

Then they see the September polls: Why, they’re cruising to victory, winning in a cakewalk. 

It’s not even close!

(No wonder they trust the polls: Not only do they say really nice things about the Dems, but they actually PAID for a lot of ‘em!)

So the candidates see the polls and are emboldened. That’s problematic, but a disciplined candidate should still be able to stick to a script. (Mostly.) 

The bigger problem is that the activists are emboldened, too. They count their chickens before they’re hatched, demanding a wish-list of left-wing policies, revenge fantasies, and political grievances — i.e. packing the Supreme Court, impeaching the president, jailing Republicans, disbanding ICE, banning billionaires, and killing the AI industry.

Historically, left-wing activists have damaged the Democratic brand more than ANYTHING Donald Trump has EVER done. They’re the GOP’s best friends.

Fast forward to 2026: Once again, the Dems dominated the month of September. (As well as August: Over the past eight years, about 70% of August polls have overestimated support for Democrats.) Once again, the Democrats have swallowed the hype.

And once again, the activists have gotten greedy.

Because of the media’s focus, left-wing rhetoric, and activist overreach, the public face of the 2026 midterms isn’t Donald Trump anymore. It certainly was in August and September, but we’re now in late October.

The public face of the 2026 midterms is now Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Ilhan Omar Ilhan Nur Said Elmi (D-Minn.)

El-Sayed simply can’t resist detonating rhetorical landmines. He has the self-restraint of a Charlie Sheen on a bender — and is terrifying normie Americans. The more media attention he absorbs, the worse it is for the rest of the Democratic Party.

Trouble is, he’s about to absorb even more: He’s attending a campaign rally Saturday with Barack Obama.

And Omar’s “not to my knowledge” gaffe when quizzed about the possibility she married her brother (!) was a gift from the political gods.

It’s the perfect PR storm because her scandal has everything: outrageous allegations, easily understood plot lines, sexual depravity, and an utterly absurd defense. You don’t have to be a political junkie to snort in derision.
